value.text: Dog lovers from across South Florida are heading to Fort Pierce this weekend for the Treasure Coast Kennel Club's Pirate Cluster, a four-day event featuring dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility, frisbee competitions, and other canine sports.The event is taking place Oct. Lucie County Fairgrounds, where visitors can watch trained canine athletes compete or give their own dogs an opportunity to try several activities. According to Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root, many of the events offer same-day participation."It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). It's fun," she said.Admission and parking are free for spectators. Fees apply for participants entering dogs into individual events.One of the most popular attractions is dock diving, where dogs run down a platform and launch themselves into a pool in pursuit of a toy.Competitors say many dogs recognize the venue before they even leave the vehicle."Once they start competing, they know what this dock means," said dock-diving participant Janet. "You'll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they'll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump."Organizers say the excitement surrounding dock diving often becomes contagious for owners and spectators alike.In addition to the sporting events, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors, raffles and opportunities for families to spend time with fellow dog lovers.The event highlights the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, build stronger relationships with their pets and connect with others in the community.Whether someone owns a highly trained competitor or simply wants to learn more about canine activities, organizers say the weekend provides an opportunity to see what these sports are all about.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite level PADI dive instructor, who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids — offering experiences that range from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons."I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" Anthony said.That curiosity grew into a deep and lasting passion."That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.The experience begins with a mermaid makeover, starting inside Anthony's custom fantasy closet — brimming with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories created just for mermaid gear."We're going to start with a mermaid makeover, which is one of my favorite parts," Anthony said. "Kate, so this is your magical closet."The closet features silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds. Accessories are on hand to complete every look."Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said.Armbands come in a variety of styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent."We have a few options if you want to go with armbands. We have these, these are super cute and they have that nice teal," Anthony said.Anthony even offered a personalized recommendation while I was browsing through the options."I think with what you are wearing I would probably wear this one," she said.Browsing the closet felt like being a kid in a candy store — wanting more of everything. Anthony said that reaction is exactly the goal."That is exactly what you should feel like," she said. "So, we'll pick out a tail, a top, some accessories, and a crown, and then we'll head over to the beach."After settling on a look — including a tail Anthony called a "wind trader" and a stunning leafy sea dragon design — I was feeling the mermaid vibe and ready for the beach.Anthony, a professional photographer for 15 years, combines breathtaking backdrops and elaborate costumes to create magic where whimsy meets the water. Once suited up, I made my way toward the water, making my mermaid marks in the sand along the way."Like a sea turtle you are going to migrate towards the ocean," she said. "And then your going to turn toward me put your fin over here — we call it a fluke."Anthony walked me through the first poses on the shoreline."The seated is the easiest first pose — you can kind of just look at the ocean and relax and let the wind take your hair," she said. "Look out towards the beach — a little water love."Next, I headed poolside for a basic mermaiding class.Anthony caters to every client's ability, even those who are a little cautious about the experience."Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said.People come to the experience for all kinds of reasons."I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," Anthony said."Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives — or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said.In the pool, Anthony was ready to teach me how to mermaid — stripping back the glam and focusing on the fundamentals."So now you've had the photoshoot and the glam and now we are going to strip it back and just have some fun swimming as a mermaid," Anthony said.She walked me through every step of the movement."So you can flex your foot up towards the top of the water and then push it down…and just do that a few times….you can feel the resistance of the water and that's what propels you," Anthony said. "I'm going to have you back float in the tail — I'll kind of help you float there."The lesson even included a dive completely underwater."3.2.1. breathe out — we dive down and then pop up," Anthony said. "That was so good — that was fun — and that's how we shoot video underwater."For Anthony, the joy of mermaiding as an adult goes far beyond the water itself. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more — some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Animal Care and Control are joining forces once again to help homeless animals find loving homes through a one-of-a-kind fundraiser.The annual Palm Beach County Fire Rescue calendar brings together firefighters, EMTs and adoptable animals for a photo shoot designed to raise money and awareness for animals in need. Organizers say the calendar has become much more than a collection of photos, helping support local animal welfare efforts while connecting pets with potential adopters.WATCH BELOW: Firefighters team up with adoptable pets for popular charity calendar fundraiserWhile posing for the camera may be outside their usual line of work, firefighters say they are happy to step out of their comfort zones for a good cause."I am excited but a little nervous, but it's for a great cause," firefighter Jose Besosa said.The fundraiser began last year and quickly gained momentum."Last year we started it, and it kind of took off from there, and it's become a huge event," said Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928.According to organizers, proceeds from the calendar benefit Palm Beach County Public Safety Animal Care and Control. Last year, the fundraiser raised $10,000, and all of the dogs featured in the calendar were adopted."Last year we raised $10,000, and we would like to double that and do what we can to help out all the animals in Palm Beach County," Bryan Brather, Second Legislative Vice President of Local 2928. said.This year's kickoff event will give the public a chance to help decide which firefighter and dog duo is featured in each month of the calendar.Some of the firefighters are already campaigning for their preferred spots."I would like a summer month because that explains why I am so hot," firefighter and EMT Trey Gilbert joked.The event is about more than fundraising. It is also an opportunity to shine a spotlight on animals looking for a second chance."There are so many dogs and cats that go through unfortunate situations. Not only because people don't want them, but because people die, and they deserve to have second chances," said Palm Beach County Fire Rescue Capt. Janice Vassalotti.The calendar kickoff event is scheduled for Sunday from 6 p.m. at Renegades in West Palm Beach. Attendees can meet firefighters, learn about adoptable animals and help determine which firefighter-and-pet pairs will represent each month of the upcoming calendar.WPTV reporter Christy Waite will be emceeing the event and announcing which firefighter and animal duo were selected for which months.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.WATCH BELOW: As execution nears, Reaves' family asks DeSantis to spare his lifeNow, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student remains in critical condition after police say he was struck by an SUV while walking to school along a construction zone in Port St. Lucie Police, the crash happened around 6 a.m. Wednesday on Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue. Investigators say the freshman was walking along the roadway, which does not have sidewalks, when a 72-year-old driver hit him from behind with an SUV. The area is currently under construction as crews work to widen a portion of Port St. Police say the driver initially believed he had struck a construction barrel. After turning around and returning to the scene, officers say he found the teen unconscious on the side of the road and called 911. Neighbors who live near the crash site say the lack of sidewalks has long been a concern, especially for students who walk or bike to school. "It's not safe to walk around here," said neighbor Kendry Portal. "We need those sidewalks." Neighbors told CBS12 News they have seen multiple crashes involving pedestrians along the busy stretch of road since construction began a few years ago. See also: Jury convicts former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard into a four-lane road and adding sidewalks as part of the ongoing project. Neighbors say the safety improvements cannot come soon enough. "I want to see this street finished as soon as possible," Portal said. Police do not believe the driver was impaired, and it remains unclear whether any charges will be filed. Authorities are asking anyone with dashcam or surveillance video from the area around the time of the crash to contact Port St. As of Thursday morning, the 14-year-old remains hospitalized in critical condition. "I just hope that he gets well soon and hope for the family in this situation," said Portal.

Lucie police confirmed that a man found unconscious in the roadway with severe head injuries early Friday morning was the victim of a hit-and-run crash.WATCH BELOW:The victim has been identified as a 63-year-old Port St. Lucie resident, police said. The incident occurred at about 12:56 a.m. near the intersection of NW University Boulevard and NW California Boulevard.The 63-year-old man was unconscious and suffering from severe head trauma and significant bleeding, police said. He was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for medical treatment and remains in critical condition.Police said detectives obtained surveillance video from a nearby business that captured the incident and are continuing to collect and evaluate additional video footage as they work to determine the circumstances surrounding the crash and identify the vehicle and driver involved.Authorities are asking anyone who was driving in the area around the time of the crash, may have witnessed the incident, or has dashcam or other video footage from the area to come forward.Even information that may seem insignificant could assist investigators in identifying the driver and bringing this investigation to a resolution. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000. The investigation remains active and ongoing.

WPTV is continuing to follow flooding issues at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. The water has receded, but earlier this week, the intersection looked like a lake.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie flooding hits pizza shop hard as city works on fixWPTV is pressing city leaders about any solution to keep the water levels down.Neighbors shared video of the roadways, looking like a river."We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," said Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria right of the intersection. "It becomes like an island around here."That island is a shopping plaza where the pizza shop is located. Due to the flooding on Thursday, Dascoli said they had to close early."It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," said Dascoli.Dascoli told WPTV customers couldn't go in and orders couldn't go out during this week’s flooding."We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," said Dascoli. "Some of our drivers, their cars aren't capable of going through the floods, so we have to stop deliveries."WPTV pressed the city of Port St. Lucie about any solutions to the flooding.Scott Samples with the city said it's starting a pilot program for water level sensors at flood-prone areas in the city."There'll be alerts that'll be able to go to Public Works and the police to say, 'Hey, this area is seeing rapid flooding,' so they might be able to respond quicker," said Samples.Samples said long-term solutions include a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood.The project includes two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect runoff, and even raising sections of the roadway at California and Savona boulevards.Right now, Samples said the project is in the data collection phase before moving on to design."This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," said Samples.

A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called. Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water. She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present. "It can be very treacherous. Ron DeSantis said two people have died and more than 430,000 customers remain without power as state and local officials begin recovery efforts following Hurricane Isaias' landfall in the Florida Panhandle.Speaking Saturday in Okaloosa County, where the Category 2 hurricane came ashore Friday night, DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, primarily from falling trees and debris.WATCH BELOW: DeSantis confirms 2 storm-related deaths in Florida Speaking from Destin, Florida, the governor said both people died in Escambia County, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons said in a video posted to Facebook that one woman died after a tree fell on her home. In a second video, Simmons said the other victim, a man, died from a generator that was not properly ventilated. The sheriff said that four other people were inside the same home and had to be hospitalized. "What I saw was both from the structural perspective, I think our structures handled the storm very well," DeSantis said. "The problem is that the storm knocked over a lot of trees."State officials confirmed two storm-related deaths. One person in Escambia County was killed when a tree fell on a home. Another person died after operating a generator inside a garage, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Emergency crews have completed roughly 180 missions through the Florida Division of Emergency Management, according to the governor. State officials said nearly 10,000 power accounts have already been restored, but approximately 430,000 customers remained without electricity Saturday morning. About 325,000 of those outages are within Florida Power & Light's service area.Officials said debris removal remains one of the biggest challenges slowing restoration efforts."The folks have been out since daylight," DeSantis said. "Some of it is that you've got to get the debris out of the way before the linemen can connect it."The Florida Department of Transportation began clearing roads and bridges before sunrise, while the Florida Highway Patrol has completed dozens of debris-clearing missions. State officials said 85 traffic signals have been restored using generators.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport has reopened to commercial air traffic, while airports in Pensacola and Fort Walton Beach remained closed Saturday but were expected to resume operations soon.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said more than 16,000 utility workers have been mobilized to restore power throughout the region.Perdue also warned residents that flooding risks remain even after the storm's passage. Several rivers, including the Shoal River in Okaloosa County, are still rising and are not expected to crest for several days."We want to make sure we keep enough resources on hand in case search and rescue is needed," Perdue said.State leaders urged residents to avoid flooded roads and standing water, warning that even shallow water can quickly become dangerous.Meanwhile, Attorney General James Uthmeier said a small number of price-gouging complaints had already been reported. Residents who believe businesses are overcharging for essentials such as fuel, food or other emergency supplies are encouraged to file complaints through the attorney general's office.Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia also warned residents about post-storm scams, including unlicensed contractors and fraudulent roofers targeting homeowners.Officials urged residents not to sign contracts or provide deposits before verifying a contractor's credentials. The state also plans to establish insurance assistance hubs in impacted areas within the next 48 hours to help residents file claims and meet with insurance representatives.Businesses affected by the storm can report damage through the state's business damage assessment survey at FloridaDisaster.biz. State officials said the information will help expedite recovery assistance and assess losses.DeSantis said recovery efforts will continue across the Panhandle, where damage stretches from the Alabama state line to the eastern Panhandle.The governor cautioned that additional flooding could develop in the coming days as rivers continue rising but said Florida has water rescue teams and emergency assets positioned throughout the region."We're going to get through this," DeSantis said. "There's damage, and that's going to be difficult for people whose property was damaged, but I also feel like this is very surmountable for us if we all just work together and get the job done."

Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm.By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday.As of 2 p.m. CT Saturday, more than 700,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 180,000 outages and Georgia reported about 40,000.At its peak, nearly 900,000 customers were without power. The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall.RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by FebruaryThe hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle.Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons confirmed one person died during the storm. He added that some roads were impassable due to downed trees and power lines. Away from the coast, a death was reported in Birmingham, Alabama, due to a fallen tree limb. Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026.Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Niño, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development.Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength.The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast.RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calmBehind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning that nearly 450,000 utility customers remained without power across Northwest Florida after Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle. Speaking from Destin later in the day, he confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.The governor said Isaias came ashore near Destin at 9:30 p.m. Friday as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of about 105 mph. Wind gusts reached as high as 116 mph near Santa Rosa Sound, while storm surge pushed water levels approximately 5.5 feet above normal in some areas.WATCH BELOW: Santa Rosa County among hardest hit counties, DeSantis saysAlthough the storm has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and moved out of Florida, DeSantis warned that flooding remains a concern, particularly in parts of the Panhandle and Big Bend expected to receive 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend."As of now there have been no confirmed fatalities," DeSantis said, noting reports of a possible death in Escambia County linked to a fallen tree had not yet been confirmed by the state.State officials said more than 16,000 linemen were staged ahead of the storm and began restoration efforts as early as 3 a.m. Saturday.By 7 a.m., approximately 448,000 customer accounts were without electricity statewide, including about 323,000 Florida Power & Light customers and roughly 110,000 customers served by electric cooperatives.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.The Florida Department of Transportation and Florida Highway Patrol launched overnight "cut and toss" operations to clear roads of fallen trees and debris. Officials said all state-owned bridges had been inspected and reopened by 6 a.m. 98, two major transportation corridors in the region, were also reopened.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport resumed commercial operations Saturday morning, while Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport and Pensacola International Airport remained closed.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said state teams remain on standby as flood risks continue."We are going to keep search and rescue teams ready to go," Perdue said. "There could be continued flooding from all of the rainfall."Officials urged residents to avoid driving through flooded roadways, stay clear of downed power lines and limit unnecessary travel while utility crews and emergency workers continue recovery efforts.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to watch for scams in the aftermath of the storm, including reports of fraudulent text messages offering tree-removal services and unlicensed contractors seeking repair work.State officials said damage assessments are underway and will help determine whether Florida qualifies for additional federal disaster aid beyond the pre-landfall emergency declaration already approved by FEMA.DeSantis said he planned to visit storm-damaged areas in the Panhandle later Saturday, including parts of Okaloosa County, to assess conditions and meet with local officials."We were ready for the worst," DeSantis said. "We'll get everything back up and running and let people go on with their lives as soon as possible."

A first-of-its-kind program is coming to Boynton Beach High School. A busy stretch of Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School will become a designated school zone after parents raised concerns about children crossing the road.WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been pressing the county, city and the Palm Beach County School District for answers. WATCH BELOW: School zone, crosswalk coming to Greenacres ElementaryBrandon and Lynn Pote reached out to Waite after growing increasingly concerned about student safety. The couple lives across from Greenacres Elementary School, where the speed limit along Haverhill Road is 40 mph, and there is currently no designated school zone or crosswalk."Right here on Haverhill Road there is no crosswalk and no school zone, and cars are going 40 mph," Brandon Pote said.The nearest guarded crosswalks are near Greenacres Christian Academy and another near 10th Avenue and Swain Boulevard.While reporting in the area, Waite witnessed some of the safety concerns families described, including children and families navigating traffic and students riding e-bikes and scooters. She also witnessed a crash along the roadway. Neighbors like Omar Trevino have lived in the area for about 20 years, and he says something needs to be done before someone gets hurt."Cars can't cross, much less kids," Trevino said.After WPTV began asking questions, Engineering and Public Works said a pedestrian safety study determined an additional crosswalk is needed along Haverhill Road to serve Greenacres Elementary School. EPW also says they are considering placing the crosswalk on Haverhill at the intersection of either Carver Street or Fourth Street. The new crosswalk will also be guarded.The City of Greenacres told WPTV it will allocate funding for the crossing guard(s) but the city will not be financially responsible for the rest of the project.But the guarded crosswalk is not the only safety change coming to the area.After Waite continued pressing the county about the lack of a designated school zone along Haverhill Road, EPW says the road will become a designated school zone.Greenacres Elementary already has a school zone along Jackson Avenue, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 mph during arrival and dismissal. However, the stretch of Haverhill Road bordering the school is not currently a designated school zone.The city also requested flashing signals or beacons to help improve visibility for students and crossing guards.For parents like Pote, the plans are welcome news after his family reached out to Waite asking for help."I watch you guys, and I see you guys do reports where you sit down and listen to the community," Pote said. "Thank you guys so much."Engineering and Public Works say they are now working to determine the location for the crosswalk and designated school zone. Once the location is determined, both are expected to be ready by early next year.The county has not said how much the project will cost.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. The family has set up a GoFundMe account for donations. A Martin County employee is being praised for her quick actions after rescuing a girl from drowning at Bob Graham Beach in Stuart on Thursday afternoon. Amy Offenbach, who came to the beach to surf, said the day took an unexpected turn. "It was just by chance that we were here and thank God that we were at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts kicked in when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water, and the beach had no lifeguards on duty. Offenbach rushed in to help, using a surfboard to stabilize the girl. "Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. Offenbach said the girl's forehead felt cold, prompting her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries. "I'm just really thankful that her parents have their child," Offenbach said. Offenbach, a Martin County employee, said she doesn’t feel the need for recognition. While some are calling her a hero, Offenbach said she was simply acting on her instincts as a mother. "I have a 14-year-old son myself, and I can't imagine him not coming back from hanging out at the beach with his friends," she said. The incident serves as a reminder to exercise caution at the beach, especially in areas without lifeguards. The award for funniest player on the Miami Dolphins goes to Ollie Gordon. Gordon is in his second year as a Dolphin, and the running back says the key to the team's potential this season comes down to what is happening inside the locker room.WATCH BELOW: Ollie Gordon sits down with WPTV sports reporter Eleanor SheahanGordon sat down with WPTV to talk about team chemistry, the competitive culture within the Dolphins' roster, his role as the locker room's self-proclaimed class clown — and why he believes this group is built to surprise people."I feel like it's going well. You know, it's getting to the basics, you know, the basics of football. I feel like we've built a good bond here. We got a new team, we got new coaches, and I feel like we're getting that brotherhood and that familyhood," Gordon said.When asked who the most competitive player in the locker room is, Gordon rattled off several names before making sure to include himself."I feel like we got a couple of people. I'm gonna say, Jordyn Brooks. He's one of the most competitive. Jacob (Rodriguez) also, Jordan Phillips, DJ Campbell. I'm gonna throw myself in there. I feel like I'm competitive too." Gordon said.Gordon said Aaron Brewer and Patrick Paul also raise the bar for the team's competitive attitude."I mean, everyone really. I feel like we just got a competitive locker room. You know, I feel like that's what makes the team. That's what makes us a good team and able to play for each other just because of stuff like that," Gordon said.Off the field, Gordon wears another title with equal pride — funniest guy on the team."I think you're looking at him. I think I can go with that. I think I can agree with that one." Gordon said.Asked why he deserves to wear that crown, Gordon was direct."Because I think that's just me. I feel like I'm always goofing around with everybody. I feel like no matter who it is, offense, defense, best teams, we're just here to have a good time," Gordon said.During practice, Gordon is uplifting his teammates and even dialing up a few handshakes with the Dolphins staff."You got to mix it up with everybody. You know, you got to get everybody ready to get everybody juice for work," Gordon said.That upbeat energy, Gordon explained, does not conflict with his competitive side; it is all about knowing when to flip the switch."I really just got to have that switch. You know, when you're in between those white lines, I feel like it's game mode. It's us versus them, you know? And then when we get outside of that, we can play around. But you know, I feel like once we're in between those white lines, those 100 yards, you know, I feel like it's go mode. We got to be ready for whatever, honestly," Gordon said.Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said Gordon is upbeat and has grown in practice and maturity on the field."I appreciate that, Coach Hafley," Gordon said. "This is a young team, and I feel like some of us all got to lead by example, even if it's not being the oldest on the team, but it's still just showing the young guys how to go. I feel like Coach Hafley has instilled that in us. Like he doesn't just talk to the vets; he talks to all of us. He tells all of us we're leaders in some way. So I feel like with him being like that, I feel like that's turned me that way."Hafley has preached all season long about growth and development. When he was asked to finish the sentence: "The Dolphins team is going to surprise people this year because...," Gordon kept the focus on unity."We stick together, and we play for each other. You know, we come out here every day. I feel like we spend so much time together that we are willing to do anything for each other. You know, and I just feel like when you go back and look, we took a bunch of games down to the wire, and in the NFL, everybody's good. Some teams get in that they hit a wall, but I feel like that's not going to be us. I feel like we're going to push through this moment and stick together as we do," Gordon said.Fans should keep an eye on the No. 0 jersey; that's Ollie Gordon.

Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard the cries of kittens buried up to 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, the sheriff revealed Friday. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided new details about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez, who is accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive at a mobile home park in Hobe Sound. According to the sheriff's office, deputies responded to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had allegedly killed two kittens Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, who feared for the safety of three remaining kittens, attempted to protect them by locking them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. Budensiek said that when the children returned home, they discovered the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were missing. The children then called law enforcement to report the incident. When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens. While speaking with deputies, Chavez said she believed the kittens had demons, described them as ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats inside the home. Chavez then led deputies to the backyard, where the kittens had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. See also: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into major Category 3 storm near Florida Panhandle As deputies dug through the backyard, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were recovered alive, while the two kittens Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property. Budensiek said the two surviving kittens were immediately taken to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries caused by a lack of oxygen while the kittens were buried. Despite being rescued, the kittens could still die from their injuries. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, according to the sheriff's office. The four charges correspond to the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. The sheriff said Chavez was being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also had an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died. The sheriff said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. Authorities also have not determined her motive. Budensiek said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the fifth kitten is found dead, according to the sheriff. Following the incident, the Florida Department of Children and Families became involved, and the children were later released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach.Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention."The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said.Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed."That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated."Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help."By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said.Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls.When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress."I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'"Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach.Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore."The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache."Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called.Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water.She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate."I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said.Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition.While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present."It can be very treacherous. Treacherous," she said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning that nearly 450,000 utility customers remained without power across Northwest Florida after Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle, but state officials had not confirmed any storm-related fatalities as recovery efforts continued. Speaking during a statewide briefing, DeSantis said the storm came ashore near Destin at 9:30 p.m. Friday as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of about 105 mph. Wind gusts reached as high as 116 mph near Santa Rosa Sound, while storm surge pushed water levels approximately 5.5 feet above normal in some areas.WATCH BELOW: Santa Rosa County among hardest hit counties, DeSantis saysAlthough the storm has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and moved out of Florida, DeSantis warned that flooding remains a concern, particularly in parts of the Panhandle and Big Bend expected to receive 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend."As of now there have been no confirmed fatalities," DeSantis said, noting reports of a possible death in Escambia County linked to a fallen tree had not yet been confirmed by the state.State officials said more than 16,000 linemen were staged ahead of the storm and began restoration efforts as early as 3 a.m. Saturday.By 7 a.m., approximately 448,000 customer accounts were without electricity statewide, including about 323,000 Florida Power & Light customers and roughly 110,000 customers served by electric cooperatives.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.The Florida Department of Transportation and Florida Highway Patrol launched overnight "cut and toss" operations to clear roads of fallen trees and debris. Officials said all state-owned bridges had been inspected and reopened by 6 a.m. 98, two major transportation corridors in the region, were also reopened.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport resumed commercial operations Saturday morning, while Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport and Pensacola International Airport remained closed.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said state teams remain on standby as flood risks continue."We are going to keep search and rescue teams ready to go," Perdue said. "There could be continued flooding from all of the rainfall."Officials urged residents to avoid driving through flooded roadways, stay clear of downed power lines and limit unnecessary travel while utility crews and emergency workers continue recovery efforts.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to watch for scams in the aftermath of the storm, including reports of fraudulent text messages offering tree-removal services and unlicensed contractors seeking repair work.State officials said damage assessments are underway and will help determine whether Florida qualifies for additional federal disaster aid beyond the pre-landfall emergency declaration already approved by FEMA.DeSantis said he planned to visit storm-damaged areas in the Panhandle later Saturday, including parts of Okaloosa County, to assess conditions and meet with local officials."We were ready for the worst," DeSantis said. "We'll get everything back up and running and let people go on with their lives as soon as possible."

Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm.By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday.As of 6 a.m. CT Saturday, more than 900,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 320,000 outages and Georgia reported about 120,000.The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall.RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by FebruaryThe hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle.Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons confirmed one person died during the storm. He added that some roads were impassable due to downed trees and power lines. Away from the coast, a death was reported in Birmingham, Alabama, due to a fallen tree limb. Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026.Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Niño, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development.Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength.The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast.RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calmBehind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. The Atlantic hurricane season typically peaks around Sept. 10 and begins to wind down by mid-October before ending Nov. 30.Since 2013, only two hurricanes have made U.S. The most recent was Hurricane Nicole in 2022.

Dog lovers from across South Florida are heading to Fort Pierce this weekend for the Treasure Coast Kennel Club's Pirate Cluster, a four-day event featuring dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility, frisbee competitions, and other canine sports.The event is taking place Oct. Lucie County Fairgrounds, where visitors can watch trained canine athletes compete or give their own dogs an opportunity to try several activities. According to Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root, many of the events offer same-day participation."It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). It's fun," she said.Admission and parking are free for spectators. Fees apply for participants entering dogs into individual events.One of the most popular attractions is dock diving, where dogs run down a platform and launch themselves into a pool in pursuit of a toy.Competitors say many dogs recognize the venue before they even leave the vehicle."Once they start competing, they know what this dock means," said dock-diving participant Janet. "You'll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they'll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump."Organizers say the excitement surrounding dock diving often becomes contagious for owners and spectators alike.In addition to the sporting events, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors, raffles and opportunities for families to spend time with fellow dog lovers.The event highlights the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, build stronger relationships with their pets and connect with others in the community.Whether someone owns a highly trained competitor or simply wants to learn more about canine activities, organizers say the weekend provides an opportunity to see what these sports are all about.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses.Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing."I would say it's about 25% higher need," she said.People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher."They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough," Mejia said. "So, that's why we're coming in and filling in the gap." The Soup Kitchen is filling in the gap for every walk of life, including employed residents, who have homes and cars but are still not making ends meet at the end of the month."You can see people from all over and we call them the household person, which is asset limited income constrained," Mejia said. "But they're employed, so they have cars, they may have a house, they may have an apartment, and it's just not adding up at the end of the month." Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food."I just come here. They have good food every day. So, I'm thank God I'm here," Marcellus said.The kitchen is able to distribute hundreds of pounds of food every day through faithful volunteers, like Mary Webb."You just feel good helping out other people and it comes back to you," Webb said. "The goodness comes back to you." The Soup Kitchen is located at 8655 W. and they can be contacted at 561-732-7595.

James Talarico has been absent from the campaign trail over the past 12 days as the Texas Senate race enters a critical stretch, prompting Republicans to open a new line of attack on the Democratic nominee.At a campaign rally in San Antonio Wednesday, Texas attorney general and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton led the crowd in a chant about his opponent’s whereabouts.“Where is James Talarico?” Paxton prompted the crowd to ask.Paxton’s campaign has also drawn attention to the topic in social media posts in recent days, and President Donald Trump has jumped into the debate on Truth Social, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION.”Talarico’s campaign said the Texas Democrat has been getting over being sick.“James looks forward to being back out this weekend after recovering from the flu,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, on Thursday. “It’s been 83 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans’ question in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do last night. Ball is in Paxton’s court.”RELATED STORY | Trump faces hecklers while making high-profile Texas campaign pushTalarico revealed his flu diagnosis September 30 when he spoke virtually with the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person.“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico told the crowd gathered in Edinburg, Texas, over video conference. “I’m running a fever, and I’m at my most contagious right now, and I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe.”Talarico’s last public appearance in Texas took place on September 26 when he held a press conference on suspending the federal gas and diesel tax and ending the war with Iran.“This is the kind of immediate action we need to provide Texans some relief at the pump in the middle of this affordability crisis,” Talarico said at a gas station in Carrollton, Texas.After publication of this story, a Talarico campaign source noted the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert De Niro on September 28.During this time stretch, Paxton has made several campaign trail stops, including speaking at Trump’s rally in San Antonio on Wednesday. Paxton has spoken at four other campaign events, including a conversation with the USHBC, and was on hand at the president’s event in Denton. At that stop, Trump said he didn’t even know Paxton was there and jokingly called him a “pain in the ass.”In a Truth Social post Wednesday night, Trump questioned Talarico’s whereabouts and called for a debate between the two Senate candidates.“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able,” Trump wrote.The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment about Trump’s proposed debate between the two candidates. Talarico has challenged Paxton to several debates, including one on Fox News, but the window for debates is narrowing with Election Day less than four weeks away.Talarico will appear at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media on Wednesday, October 14 in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton.The two candidates are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat currently occupied by GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who Paxton defeated in a bruising Republican primary in May.RELATED STORY | Republicans fret as Talarico bombards airwaves and Paxton awaits Trump team’s cashA recent New York Times/Siena University poll showed Talarico with a six-point lead over Paxton.The close nature of the race in a state Trump won by double digits in 2024 is causing anxiety for Republicans, who are flooding the Texas airwaves in the final stretch. GOP ad spending in the state from September to November currently stands at more than $190 million compared to $52 million spent by Democrats during the same time period.

(CBS12) The American Red Cross assisted five people, including two children, following two house fires in Palm Beach and St. According to a news release issued Friday, Oct. 9, Red Cross Disaster Action Team volunteers responded to both fires within a 12-hour period. The fires occurred at two locations: ● Riviera Beach: A home on West 28th Street, where one adult received assistance. Lucie: A home on Northwest Carmelite Street, where four people, including two adults and two children, received assistance. Red Cross volunteers provided emergency financial assistance, health and mental health services, and recovery support to those affected. The organization’s Disaster Action Team consists of specially trained volunteers who respond to emergencies 24 hours a day, seven days a week, providing resources and support to families impacted by disasters. All Red Cross disaster assistance is provided free of charge through donations. The Red Cross did not release information about what caused either fire or the extent of the damage. Residents interested in supporting disaster relief efforts can donate at redcross.org/donate. Information about home fire safety and preparedness is available at redcross.org/homefires.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere.
