MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the transit system without regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. Martin County officials told WPBF's Caleb Califano they were given no advance warning that service would stop Thursday. According to the county, MARTY’s operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract. The company says rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs have led to significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Despite negotiations with the county, the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. County officials said the company provided a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. However, Thursday morning, Martin County Transit LLC notified the county that it was immediately discontinuing service. The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. Riders react Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for the bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never came. She was unaware that the MARTY bus had been suspended until WPBF's Jasimine Yasmine Julmisse informed her. Chaclain says she's been riding the bus for years and that it's a staple for many members of the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don’t have a driver’s license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It’s very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don’t drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don’t drive, and we go everywhere to shop." The sudden suspension of service impacted riders including Steven Godell, who said he was on his bicycle Thursday because he didn't see the MARTY bus come Thursday morning. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm.By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday.As of 6 a.m. CT Saturday, more than 900,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 320,000 outages and Georgia reported about 120,000.The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall.RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by FebruaryThe hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle.No deaths or injuries associated with the storm had been reported as of early Saturday morning.Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026.Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Niño, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development.Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength.The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast.RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calmBehind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. The Atlantic hurricane season typically peaks around Sept. 10 and begins to wind down by mid-October before ending Nov. 30.Since 2013, only two hurricanes have made U.S. The most recent was Hurricane Nicole in 2022.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday night with 105 mph winds.Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news conference a short time later that power outages spanned from Pensacola to Panama City to Tallahassee.Watch update from Governor DeSantis:"(Power) crews will be mobilizing once the storm passes, and they will be hard at work as soon as it's safe to do so and they have the light to be able to operate," DeSantis said Friday night.Ahead of the storm, the governor on Friday warned that storm surge would impact a large stretch of the Gulf Coast, extending well beyond the immediate landfall area.While residents in areas such as Destin and neighboring communities faced the greatest surge threat, officials said coastal flooding could reach as far east as Apalachicola and potentially affect portions of the Tampa Bay region because of the storm's large size."You're going to see water across the entire region of the Florida Panhandle," DeSantis said.Officials cautioned that hazards will not be limited to communities near the eye of the storm. Tornadoes could develop far from the center, including in Tallahassee and other parts of North Florida, while heavy rain bands are expected to continue through Saturday."There will be impacts from this far, far outside the National Hurricane Center's cone," DeSantis said.State Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said dangerous conditions had already begun for some communities."The time to prepare has passed," Perdue said. "For many of you, if you're there, it's time to shelter in place and stay safe."Evacuation orders remain in effect across multiple Panhandle counties, particularly for barrier islands, low-lying areas and RV parks. Officials urged residents who are still able to leave evacuation zones to do so immediately.State crews have staged significant resources ahead of the storm, including more than 1,400 generators, fuel, food and water supplies and thousands of emergency responders.The state has also positioned 16,000 utility workers to begin restoring power once conditions are safe."We do anticipate extensive power outages here," DeSantis said.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 5,000 service members and more than 1,300 high-water vehicles. Search-and-rescue teams, helicopters, boats and other specialized equipment have been pre-positioned throughout the region.More than 6,000 linemen and restoration personnel are standing by to support power restoration efforts following Hurricane Isaias.The Florida State Guard has deployed nearly 400 soldiers to assist with pre-landfall and post-landfall efforts, including preliminary damage assessments, route clearance, points of distribution operations, and air, ground, and maritime search and rescue support.Transportation disruptions are also expected. Officials said Florida Highway Patrol may close portions of Interstate 10 and other major roadways and bridges once winds exceed 39 mph. Multiple airports, including Pensacola International Airport and airports in Destin and Fort Walton Beach, have announced closures.State officials also warned residents not to drive through flooded roadways and to stay away from downed power lines after the storm passes.Attorney General James Uthmeier warned that looting and price gouging during the emergency will be aggressively prosecuted."Don't even try it," Uthmeier said. "During emergencies, there's heightened penalties."Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia encouraged residents to document their homes and belongings before the storm by taking photos and videos and storing records digitally for insurance purposes.Officials emphasized that residents should be prepared to be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours after the storm and reminded generator users never to operate generators inside homes because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.As Isaias approaches, emergency managers are asking Floridians to follow local evacuation orders, monitor weather alerts and avoid travel once conditions deteriorate."We're ready for it," DeSantis said. "We just got to get through it."Currently, 27 Florida counties are under a state of emergency.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesList of shelter locationsSchool Closures around the Big BendLatest list on sandbag locationsWant to see more local news?

Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone. Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it. During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

Bryant told the officers that the dog was hers, and that he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach.Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention."The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said.Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed."That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated."Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help."By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said.Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls.When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress."I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'"Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach.Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore."The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache."Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called.Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water.She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate."I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said.Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition.While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present."It can be very treacherous. Treacherous," she said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The Florida Department of Health in Indian River County has issued a 60-day rabies alert after a bat captured near the Sonrise Apartments tested positive for the virus.Health officials said the bat was captured in the Sonrise Apartments area off Sonrise Place in Fellsmere on Sept. Anyone who may have had contact with or touched the bat is urged to contact the Department of Health in Indian River County at 772-794-7472.WATCH BELOW: Rabid bat prompts alert in Indian River CountyThe alert comes as health officials monitor rabies activity among wild animals in the area and warn residents that the disease is present in the local wildlife population.Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of mammals, including humans. Health officials say people who are exposed to rabies can protect themselves by seeking prompt medical treatment after exposure.The Department of Health is reminding residents and visitors to avoid contact with wild animals such as raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats and coyotes, which are more likely to carry the disease.Officials also recommend taking several precautions to reduce the risk of exposure, including:Keeping pets vaccinated against rabiesSupervising pets and keeping them on a leashSecuring livestock on private propertyAvoiding contact with wild or stray animals, including catsNot feeding or handling wildlifePreventing bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildingsAnyone bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Indian River County at 772-794-7472.If a pet or livestock animal is bitten by another animal, owners should contact a veterinarian immediately and notify Indian River County Animal Control at 772-226-4799.Visit the Florida Department of Health website for more information on rabies.

A 17-year-old died after being shot near a boat ramp in Indian River County late Friday night, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.Deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the 3700 block of County Road 512, near Garcia's Boat Ramp, at approximately 11:24 p.m.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampThe sheriff's office said deputies found the 17-year-old and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived.The teen was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center before being flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center, where he died from his injuries.Detectives with the sheriff's office's Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel are processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses.Investigators said the shooting appears to be an isolated incident and there is no threat to the public.No information about a possible suspect or what led up to the shooting has been released.Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.The investigation remains active.

No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday.WATCH BELOW: Sheriff Eric Flowers give update on shooting death of teen"We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said.The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp."The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch," Flowers said. "He's going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case."The teen's friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries.The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff's office's Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene.WATCH: 17-year-old dies after shooting near Garcia's Boat RampFlowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed."There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there's going to be more of this." Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene.During Monday's news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim's mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School.The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia's Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance."When it's Snapchat, it's basically a private conversation," Flowers said. "But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there."Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger."Now we're adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead."The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention."The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that," Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups."With Vero Beach High School's homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children's whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff's office."Parents, if your kids are telling you that they're headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they're going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us," Flowers said.He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward."I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people," Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they're going to have to be accountable for that."Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff's Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

Governor Ron DeSantis was in Indian River County on Monday to celebrate the completion of a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road, a $100 million project state officials say will improve traffic flow, emergency response times and freight movement.The interchange, which opened about a year ahead of schedule, marks the first new I-95 interchange built in Indian River County in nearly 50 years.DeSantis said the project will provide a new direct connection to I-95 while easing congestion at nearby interchanges at Indrio Road and State Road 60."This is going to bring a new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit," DeSantis said.According to the governor, drivers using Oslo Road to access I-95 can expect travel times to be cut roughly in half. State transportation officials also project traffic along the corridor will continue growing through 2045.DeSantis said the project is expected to have significant public safety benefits as well. The state estimates emergency response times in the area could be reduced by as much as 56%, allowing first responders to reach crashes and other emergencies more quickly."This will ultimately save some lives because time is of the essence in some of these situations," DeSantis said.Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said improved access to I-95 for first responders was one of the project's most important features."Every single second counts when it comes to saving lives, and this is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially," Perdue said.The new interchange is also expected to improve freight movement for businesses in southern Indian River County by providing a more direct route to the interstate for trucks and commercial traffic.State officials said the project was accelerated through Florida's Moving Florida Forward initiative, a transportation funding program launched by the DeSantis administration to speed up major road projects across the state.Perdue said FDOT worked with contractors through a "voluntary acceleration" program that rewarded construction teams for finding ways to complete projects more quickly. As a result, the Oslo Road interchange was finished approximately 400 days ahead of schedule.In addition to transportation improvements, FDOT acquired land near the interchange to establish a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. State officials said the site will serve as the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida, allowing protected tortoises to be moved while infrastructure projects continue.The Oslo Road interchange is part of nearly $1 billion in planned transportation investments across Florida's Treasure Coast region."This interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future," DeSantis said.

A new ammunition manufacturing facility in Indiantown is bringing additional manufacturing activity and planned job growth to Martin County as the Treasure Coast continues to contend with unemployment rates above the statewide average.Ikonick Energetics recently expanded its operations into Indiantown, opening a primer manufacturing facility that is part of the company’s broader ammunition production operation in Martin County.Richard Rhatigan, vice president of law enforcement and government sales at Ikonick USA, said the facility has significant production capacity.“At full capacity you're looking at a billion primers per year,” said Rhatigan.Primers are a small part of the larger puzzle in manufacturing ammunition. “It is one of the four components that go into building ammunition, so the primer actually ignites the powder which is incased within the brass,” said Rhatigan.While cameras were not permitted inside the primer manufacturing facility, Ikonick provided a look at its ammunition manufacturing operation in Stuart.At the Stuart facility, workers combine the primer, brass casing and projectile to produce finished ammunition.With the addition of the Indiantown facility, the company says about 75% of each piece of ammunition is now produced in Martin County.Ikonick also plans to hire over 100 additional employees across its two locations. The positions are expected to include both entry-level and more specialized manufacturing jobs.“When you talk about American manufacturing what that really means is, the people who work in our facilities, they live in our community,” said Rhatigan.The company says the expansion reflects the potential for additional manufacturing growth in the area.“The opportunity for expansion is here and it is part of supporting the community in Martin County,” said Rhatigan.The Indiantown Chamber of Commerce said the new facility represents a significant investment in advanced manufacturing for the region.The company also says its Martin County operations will help meet ammunition needs for law enforcement training.“We can support the state and local law enforcement training needs with our ammo with our facility in Stuart and here in Indiantown,” said Rhatigan.The expansion comes as Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties report unemployment rates above the statewide average, according to the latest unemployment data.For Indiantown, the facility represents another addition to the community’s manufacturing sector and could provide new employment opportunities as Ikonick continues to expand its operations.Portions of this story were assisted by artificial intelligence tools and reviewed by a WPTV journalists to ensure accuracy, clarity, and adherence to editorial standards.

Despite regulations requiring it, an air traffic controller failed to tell the pilots of an Amazon cargo plane about the potential for strong tail winds as they landed in Miami, careening off the runway and killing five people last month, according to a preliminary report Thursday from the National Transportation Safety Board.Just four minutes before clearing the plane for landing, an air traffic controller had provided a wind advisory to a different flight, noting gusts of up to 25 mph from the south. But the controller “did not issue information about the wind” to the pilots of the Amazon cargo plane, the report said.According to federal regulations, “both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tail wind component exists,” the NTSB report said.The preliminary report did not list a cause of the crash. The ongoing investigation could take more than a year to complete.The airplane, carrying packages of contact lenses for Amazon, came in fast after a flight from Puerto Rico and barreled roughly 1,200 feet past the end of the runway at Miami International Airport on Sept. It smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes. Five people who were in the van died. Two others in the van sustained serious injuries, as did the driver of a car that was hit by the plane. The two pilots had minor injuries.RELATED STORY | 5 dead after Amazon cargo aircraft overruns runway in Miami, striking multiple vehiclesTail winds can make landing a plane harderExperts said it appears the weather played at least some role in the accident. Tail winds can make it harder to slow a plane and push it past an ideal landing spot on a runway.“When you’ve got winds like that, it is your responsibility as a controller to issue that to a pilot, especially on landing and especially when you have gusts,” said Tony Mello, a former Federal Aviation Administration official who oversaw air traffic control services in the central U.S.Landing with a gusting tail wind “requires more concentration on the part of the pilot” but is not impossible, said former NTSB member John Goglia.Failing to share the wind conditions “was a significant omission but, in and of itself, would not have caused a crash,” Goglia said. “Every crash is a chain of events. That’s just one event.”The plane had little runway left when it touched downA summary of cockpit voice recordings previously released by the NTSB said one of the pilots repeatedly warned his counterpart that they were going too fast as they approached for landing and after touchdown. But the fellow pilot never gave “a consistent verbal response” to the warnings, the NTSB said. The two pilots had flown together for the first time just earlier that day, according to the preliminary NTSB report.The cockpit audio recordings also captured a series of automated warnings from the plane about the speed of descent and the approaching terrain.When it touched down, the plane was traveling at 184 mph and was already about three-quarters of a mile past the start of the runway, the NTSB report said.The pilots may have tried too late to abort the landing. Data from the plane show its wheel brakes were applied, then released as the engines throttled to “go-around” thrust values before the brakes again were applied with about 415 feet of runway remaining.The plane ran off the pavement while still traveling at 130 mph, then struck some airport equipment and the cleaning crew’s van before crashing through a perimeter fence, hitting a car on a public road and coming to rest with its nose in a parking lot fence, the preliminary report said.RELATED STORY | Amazon suspends use of 21 Air, the cargo carrier whose plane careened off Miami runway and killed 5Plane's operator says it is focused on safetyAfter the crash, Amazon suspended its partnership with 21 Air, which operated the plane. The North Carolina carrier had flown packages for Amazon since 2024. The Boeing 767 that crashed was 32 years old and originally built to carry passengers. It was converted to a cargo plane in June 2016, the preliminary NTSB report said.The plane’s operator, 21 Air, said in a written statement Thursday that safety is “a core focus” of its organization.“We are reviewing the information in the NTSB preliminary report closely, alongside our own internal safety and operational protocols, and we will take all appropriate action to improve our safety based on the facts as they are established,” the company said.The Miami crash came less than a year after a UPS cargo plane crashed at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway. That crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

A 10th-grade student and another person were killed after a multi-vehicle crash involving a school bus happened Monday morning in Central Florida. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news conference that the crash happened around 6 a.m., when a Chevrolet Malibu veered over the center line of a road and hit a Winter Haven High School bus traveling in the opposite direction. There were 37 students on board. The impact of the collision ripped the tire off the bus and caused it to crash head-on into an oncoming Jeep before rolling over off the side of Winter Haven Road. The sheriff said the driver of the Jeep had died. At least five other people involved in the crash were hospitalized, according to authorities. "It was a horrible crash," Judd said. "It was a terrible, tragic morning. We had a beautiful 10th grade girl lose her life."The city of Winter Haven is located about 51 miles east of Tampa and 47 miles southwest of Orlando.This story was originally published by Leilyn Torres and Anthony Romano with the Scripps News Group in Tampa.

Florida's minimum wage increased on Sept. This is the fourth and last of the annual scheduled hikes from a 2020 approved referendum. The minimum wage for tipped workers also rose to $11.98.WATCH BELOW: Florida minimum wage hits $15/hour "Minimum wage is going up but so is everything going up," a young man named Neff told me Wednesday on Clematis Street. "You have to have another hustle, or another job so that way you can create more revenue and income for your family; $15 an hour is not enough." Starting in 2027, the state minimum wage will be adjusted for inflation annually. In South Florida, where the cost of living is high, a $25-an-hour wage is considered "livable," according to a Massachusetts Institute of Technology report. The higher wage can also mean more pressure on small businesses. "I have to pass that cost on to the consumer; I cannot absorb a 7% increase in labor," John Ries, owner of Hot Pie Pizza in West Palm Beach, said. Ries says that, as a policy, he pays his employees above the minimum wage, and he admits inflation on all aspects of his business make it tough to keep prices down.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday night with 105 mph winds.Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a news conference a short time later that power outages spanned from Pensacola to Panama City to Tallahassee.Watch update from Governor DeSantis: "(Power) crews will be mobilizing once the storm passes, and they will be hard at work as soon as it's safe to do so and they have the light to be able to operate," DeSantis said Friday night. Ahead of the storm, the governor on Friday warned that storm surge would impact a large stretch of the Gulf Coast, extending well beyond the immediate landfall area.While residents in areas such as Destin and neighboring communities faced the greatest surge threat, officials said coastal flooding could reach as far east as Apalachicola and potentially affect portions of the Tampa Bay region because of the storm's large size."You're going to see water across the entire region of the Florida Panhandle," DeSantis said.Officials cautioned that hazards will not be limited to communities near the eye of the storm. Tornadoes could develop far from the center, including in Tallahassee and other parts of North Florida, while heavy rain bands are expected to continue through Saturday."There will be impacts from this far, far outside the National Hurricane Center's cone," DeSantis said.State Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said dangerous conditions had already begun for some communities."The time to prepare has passed," Perdue said. "For many of you, if you're there, it's time to shelter in place and stay safe."Evacuation orders remain in effect across multiple Panhandle counties, particularly for barrier islands, low-lying areas and RV parks. Officials urged residents who are still able to leave evacuation zones to do so immediately.State crews have staged significant resources ahead of the storm, including more than 1,400 generators, fuel, food and water supplies and thousands of emergency responders.The state has also positioned 16,000 utility workers to begin restoring power once conditions are safe."We do anticipate extensive power outages here," DeSantis said.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 5,000 service members and more than 1,300 high-water vehicles. Search-and-rescue teams, helicopters, boats and other specialized equipment have been pre-positioned throughout the region.More than 6,000 linemen and restoration personnel are standing by to support power restoration efforts following Hurricane Isaias.The Florida State Guard has deployed nearly 400 soldiers to assist with pre-landfall and post-landfall efforts, including preliminary damage assessments, route clearance, points of distribution operations, and air, ground, and maritime search and rescue support.Transportation disruptions are also expected. Officials said Florida Highway Patrol may close portions of Interstate 10 and other major roadways and bridges once winds exceed 39 mph. Multiple airports, including Pensacola International Airport and airports in Destin and Fort Walton Beach, have announced closures.State officials also warned residents not to drive through flooded roadways and to stay away from downed power lines after the storm passes.Attorney General James Uthmeier warned that looting and price gouging during the emergency will be aggressively prosecuted."Don't even try it," Uthmeier said. "During emergencies, there's heightened penalties."Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia encouraged residents to document their homes and belongings before the storm by taking photos and videos and storing records digitally for insurance purposes.Officials emphasized that residents should be prepared to be self-sufficient for at least 72 hours after the storm and reminded generator users never to operate generators inside homes because of the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.As Isaias approaches, emergency managers are asking Floridians to follow local evacuation orders, monitor weather alerts and avoid travel once conditions deteriorate."We're ready for it," DeSantis said. "We just got to get through it."Currently, 27 Florida counties are under a state of emergency.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesList of shelter locationsSchool Closures around the Big BendLatest list on sandbag locationsWant to see more local news?

Ron DeSantis signed an executive order Tuesday issuing a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of Hurricane Isaias.The counties included are: Baker, Bay, Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gilchrist, Gulf, Hamilton, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Leon, Liberty, Madison, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Suwannee, Taylor, Walton, Wakulla, and Washington.TRACKING THE TROPICS: Hurricane Center | Hurricane Guide“Today, I signed an Executive Order issuing a state of emergency ahead of potential impacts from Tropical Depression 9. This order will allow the Florida Division of Emergency Management to stage critical preparedness resources and ensure Florida is ready to respond,” DeSantis said.The governor urged Floridians to make disaster plans and check hurricane supplies.The current forecast indicates a tropical storm or hurricane could make landfall somewhere along the central Gulf Coast later this week, the governor said in a Tuesday statement."Impacts are expected to extend beyond the point of landfall, with heavy rainfall, strong winds, coastal flooding and isolated tornadoes possible across North Florida," the statement said. Ron DeSantis announced Tuesday that Florida's intensified effort to root out fraud, waste and abuse in the state's Medicaid program has resulted in more than $1 billion in projected savings and the removal of hundreds of providers from the system.Speaking at the Healthcare District of Palm Beach County alongside Agency for Health Care Administration (AHCA) Secretary Shevaun Harris, DeSantis said the state has expanded oversight and enforcement measures to identify fraudulent billing and improper Medicaid payments.WATCH BELOW: State targets Medicaid fraud, removes hundreds of providers"We want to make sure that what is being spent is being spent well," DeSantis said. "Medicaid dollars must go to healthcare for eligible Floridians, not to people who are gaming the system."According to state officials, AHCA has conducted more than 400 provider site visits since January and increased the use of data analytics, claims monitoring and background screening to uncover suspicious activity.As part of the crackdown, the state said more than 150 fraud-related referrals have been made to the Florida Attorney General's Office over the past year, more than 250 providers have been placed on payment restrictions or had payments suspended, and more than 220 providers have been terminated from Florida Medicaid due to fraud, waste or abuse.State officials said those terminated providers accounted for more than $230 million in Medicaid billing in 2025.A major focus of the effort has been Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA) services, commonly used to help children with autism. According to Harris, Florida Medicaid spent approximately $6.57 billion on ABA services between 2023 and 2025, nearly four times more than any other state's Medicaid program. At one point, spending was projected to grow by 30% annually.The state moved ABA services into managed care in 2025, a change officials say has improved oversight and slowed spending growth to less than 10% annually. As a result, the state now projects ABA-related expenditures at roughly $2.8 billion, more than $1 billion lower than previous forecasts."That is where we want our funding going," Harris said. "Not in the pockets of crooks."Investigators uncovered instances in which providers billed Medicaid for impossible service schedules, including claims for more than 24 hours of care in a single day and services allegedly provided continuously through weekends and holidays.To strengthen provider screening, AHCA also partnered with identity verification company SentiLink to help identify synthetic identities, suspicious ownership structures and other potential fraud indicators before providers enter the Medicaid system.In July, WPTV chief investigator Jamie Ostroff spoke with families in Palm Beach County whose access to ABA was abruptly cut off by Medicaid. They told her ABA was a lifeline for their children who were able to learn in school, communicate, use the bathroom and control tantrums thanks to the therapy.Despite the enforcement actions, DeSantis and Harris emphasized that the effort is aimed at fraudulent providers and not families who rely on Medicaid services.When Ostroff asked about concerns from families struggling to access ABA therapy, particularly in Palm Beach County, DeSantis replied, "If you have a provider that is doing some legitimate services and much fraudulent — to the extent that those services get interrupted, that's not AHCA's fault. That's that provider's fault."Harris added that managed care plans are working with affected recipients to connect them with new providers when a provider is removed from the program."If there is a parent watching and they're having any issues, they can contact the agency and we will help them ourselves or connect them with their managed care plan," Harris said.DeSantis said the Medicaid initiative is part of a broader effort to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly while maintaining Florida's fiscal position. The governor highlighted the state's recent budget reductions, debt repayment efforts and tax relief measures as examples of what he described as responsible financial management.State officials said AHCA will continue conducting site visits, monitoring claims and referring suspected fraud cases for further investigation.Ostroff asked Harris for a list of providers accused of fraud. She said she would provide what she could without jeopardizing any ongoing, potentially criminal, investigations."This is kind of just the opening salvo," DeSantis said. "I would anticipate you will see more results coming in the weeks, months and years ahead."

Florida officials are urging residents in the Panhandle to finalize their hurricane preparations as Hurricane Isaias strengthens in the Gulf of Mexico and heads toward the state's northwestern coast.During a news briefing Thursday, Gov. Ron DeSantis said the storm is expected to bring impacts as early as Friday afternoon, with landfall projected late Friday night into early Saturday morning.WATCH THE FULL NEWS CONFERENCE BELOW: While forecasters currently expect Isaias to make landfall as a Category 2 hurricane, state officials said they are preparing for a Category 3 storm."We're taking it very seriously," DeSantis said. "Our assumption is that it's going to hit strong as a probably lower-end Category 3, and then we work off that assumption."The governor warned that the storm's most dangerous conditions are expected to be on the eastern side of its track, putting much of the Florida Panhandle at risk for storm surge, tornadoes, flooding and damaging winds.Current forecasts show landfall somewhere between Mobile Bay and Navarre, though officials stressed the track could still change.State emergency officials said storm surge of 5 to 7 feet is possible along portions of the Panhandle. Evacuation orders have already been issued in several counties, primarily for Zones A and B, barrier islands and other low-lying areas."We want everybody to be prepared," DeSantis said. "There will be impacts all across the Florida Panhandle."Florida's Emergency Operations Center is operating at its highest activation level as agencies across the state prepare for response and recovery efforts.The Florida Division of Emergency Management has staged more than 1,000 generators, 500,000 gallons of gasoline, 1 million gallons of diesel fuel, more than 3 million meals ready to eat and 1.1 million bottles of water.More than 6,000 utility workers and restoration personnel are standing by to respond to power outages.The Florida Department of Transportation has also mobilized 900 personnel, nearly 260 pieces of heavy equipment and 100 pumps ahead of the storm. Tolls have been suspended on several Panhandle roadways to help facilitate evacuations and emergency response.Officials said approximately 5,000 members of the Florida National Guard are being activated, while the Florida State Guard has deployed 175 soldiers, aircraft and rescue vessels to support storm operations.Search-and-rescue assets, including airboats, shallow-water boats, swamp buggies and high-water vehicles, have also been pre-positioned throughout the anticipated impact area.Emergency managers said one of the biggest concerns is the potential for inland flooding.The Panhandle has already experienced significant rainfall in recent weeks, leaving many areas saturated before the storm's arrival."You're going to see rising water," DeSantis said. "You're going to see these interior places that I discussed."Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said officials are closely monitoring rivers, streams and drainage systems that could overflow as additional rain falls."We're viewing this as it could be a Category 3 major hurricane, and we want to be prepared for that," Perdue said.Officials are encouraging residents to complete preparations immediately, including filling gas tanks, securing supplies and reviewing evacuation plans.DeSantis said residents in the storm's path should assume power outages are likely and be prepared with enough water and nonperishable food to last several days.Emergency managers also reminded residents not to leave pets behind during evacuations. Every county in Florida has at least one pet-friendly shelter, officials said.Residents are encouraged to follow guidance from local emergency management agencies and heed all evacuation orders."Do not wait until conditions deteriorate to take action," Perdue said. "Make decisions now to keep yourself and your family safe."Officials also cautioned residents who plan to use generators after the storm to operate them outdoors and away from enclosed spaces to avoid potentially deadly carbon monoxide poisoning.The state said preparations and resource staging will continue as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast, with tropical-storm-force winds expected before landfall and hazardous conditions likely continuing into Saturday.

The political committee supporting Amendment 3 — which would raise Florida's homestead tax exemption — received an $18 million cash infusion in September, campaign finance records show. The two committees opposing the amendment raised a combined $680,000, a margin of more than 26 to 1.In the coming days and weeks, voters can expect to see significant messaging urging a "yes" vote on the amendment.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 backers outraise opponents 26-to-1Digging deeper into those campaign finance records, I found the "No" committees received donations from numerous corporate, individual and nonprofit contributors. Yes on 3's $18 million came from a single source: Florida Realtors.Margy Grant is the chief executive of Florida Realtors and the sole contributor to "Yes on 3.""As the voice of real estate, Florida Realtors is a longtime advocate for homeowners," Grant said. "Families are struggling with the affordability of so many things. When you go to the grocery store, when you go to the gas station, prices just continue to climb. The one thing we can possibly control is property taxes." Jackson Peel, spokesman for "Floridians for Shared Prosperity" — one of the two "No" groups — said his side has an advantage despite the funding gap."Well, we have the advantage of the facts on our side," Peel said. "This is not the savings that is promised on the mailers in your mailbox from the realtors— that this is a scam and a tax shift. You're gonna end up paying more in other ways."While the political committees against Amendment 3 have a much smaller war chest, Peel said Florida voters are still hearing their warnings through opposition from groups like the Florida Sheriff's Association and the Florida Association of Firefighters."I'm on the side of the sheriffs, the police, and the firefighters who say that this is bad for our community's public safety. I'm on the side of the teachers who say, yeah, this is gonna cut after-school programs that help our kids." Peel said.On the question of funding for public services, Grant said she has full confidence in elected officials."If you look at the increase in revenue over the past 10 years, it has doubled. Services have not doubled," Grant said. "I have full faith and confidence in our elected officials that they will be able to implement Amendment 3 successfully and effectively." A constitutional amendment requires approval by 60 percent of voters to pass. Pete Polls found 45 percent of likely voters support Amendment 3, 30 percent oppose it, and 25 percent say they are undecided.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A Boca Raton man is bringing light to his community after helping raise money to house a homeless man.John Ferber is behind the good deed and said his act was inspired by a video on social media. Ferber spotted Peter Martin at a bus stop bench months ago and decided to approach him.WATCH BELOW: WPTV's Zitlali Solache speaks with Ferber and Martin"I just had some free time and I decided to grab some Chinese food," said Ferber. “I drove up to Peter and sure enough, he was on the bench where I thought he would be, and we had a great conversation."Ferber learned Martin lost his job back in 2023, leaving him homeless. Ferber started a GoFundMe to help Martin find a studio apartment and quickly raised nearly $4,000."I've gone through a lot, days and days, 5,6,7, days without eating at times," said Martin. Fresh new start."With the funds collected by Ferber, Martin will move into a studio apartment on Wednesday. Martin adds that the gift came just in time, as he celebrated his 67th birthday on Monday."It was my birthday and John pulled up," said Martin. "He hit me with that big gift and never in my life has anybody been that forthcoming and gracious and hospitable, giving generously," said Martin.During his time in the streets, Martin suffered two heart attacks. Martin adds he was once a chef and hopes to get back to his craft."I hope to get the job and use what I've been using for 45-50 years as far as skill and knowledge and bring some value to a business," said Martin.For Ferber, it's only the beginning of his acts of kindness and his friendship with Peter. He hopes his good deed creates a domino effect in his community."Peter, I love you. I know that this is the first step to the best next year and the rest of your life," said Ferber. Body camera video captured the moments on Sunday morning when a Riviera Beach officer helped a family of four escape their home after their truck caught fire.Officer Andrew Hinds spoke with WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache about how it all happened.WATCH BELOW: Officers alert family after truck fire threatens homeHinds called it a case of being at the right place, at the right time."Honestly, I'm just relieved that everybody got out and it didn’t spread anymore," said Hinds.Hinds was on regular patrol duty at about 10 a.m. when he noticed smoke."While we were doing traffic, we looked up and saw smoke coming from a house," said Hinds.Officers rushed towards the house and found a truck engulfed in flames."Residents were flagging us down, telling us there were people inside; some small kids and a family," said Hinds.Hinds was the one to call dispatch and notify them of the truck fire. An anonymous donation expected to exceed $50 million is helping cover tuition costs for medical laboratory science students at the University of Washington for the next half-century.The dean of the university's School of Medicine, Dr. Tim Dellit, made the surprise announcement Monday to about 30 grateful undergrads, who will each see two quarters' worth of tuition covered for their senior-year clinical rotations, The Seattle Times reported."I'm really shocked," said Jasmine Wertz, eyes filling with tears. Coco Gauff came back to defeat Ons Jabeur 4-6, 6-2, 6-3 at the French Open on Tuesday to reach the semifinals at a third consecutive Grand Slam tournament.Gauff won her first major title at the U.S. Open in September, then made it to the final four at the Australian Open in January.The 20-year-old American is seeded No. 3 at Roland Garros, where she was the runner-up to Iga Swiatek in 2022.Gauff could get a rematch in the semifinals against the top-ranked Swiatek, who has won three of the past four titles in Paris.Swiatek’s quarterfinal against 2023 Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova was scheduled for later Tuesday on Court Philippe Chatrier.Jabeur's mix of speeds and spins gave Gauff fits at times. And as well-known as Gauff is for her ability to cover the court and play defense, Jabeur managed to keep coming up with winners, finishing with 30 in all.“She was playing really well the whole match. She was hitting a lot of winners on me, which is something I’m not used to against anybody,” Gauff said. “So today I was just trying to just be aggressive toward the end.”Gauff pulled away to a 5-2 lead in the last set, then needed a trio of match points to close things out, acknowledging afterward that maybe she grew a little tight down the stretch. The last game was key, with Gauff needing to save a break point, then Jabeur dismissing one match point with a disguised drop shot that earned a roar from the stands that the 29-year-old Tunisian responded to by putting her right index finger to her ear.But on Gauff's next opportunity to seal the victory, Jabeur badly flubbed an overhead. Gauff smiled, then raised her arms and yelled.With the crowd at the main stadium loudly supporting Jabeur at times, Gauff did not play badly in the opening set. 8 seed Jabeur — a three-time major finalist — was superb, winning 17 of 18 first-serve points, never facing a single break point and accumulating a 12-5 edge in total winners.When she delivered an ace at 114 mph (184 kph) to end the set, Jabeur nodded repeatedly.“She’s a tough opponent and she’s well-loved on tour. I could tell by the crowd today — I know you guys wanted her to win. Honestly, whenever she’s not playing (me), I cheer for her, too,” Gauff said.“Even though you guys were for Ons, I really had a lot of fun, even when I lost the first set and they were chanting when I was in the bathroom," Gauff said about her trip off the court after the first set. "I was like, ‘This is just really fun, win or lose.’ It is.”Gauff got going after that, raising her level and trying to gain the upper hand during lengthier exchanges. She put in 16 winners over the last two sets, while breaking serve four times.“I know I have a lot of love here in Paris. Trust me, I know," said Gauff, who won the French Open junior title at age 14. "So I really appreciate it, and hopefully you guys can help me make it through the next round.”

The criminal charges against world No. 1 golfer Scottie Scheffler have been dismissed following his arrest earlier this month at the PGA Championship in Louisville, Kentucky."Based upon the totality of the evidence, my office cannot move forward in the prosecution of the charges filed against Mr. Scheffler," Jefferson County Attorney Mike O'Connell said at a brief hearing Wednesday. Scheffler's actions and the evidence surrounding their exchange during the misunderstanding do not satisfy the elements of any criminal offenses," O'Connell added. The judge then accepted his motion to have the charges dismissed.Scheffler, 27, was taken into custody by Louisville Police on May 17 outside Valhalla Golf Club ahead of the second round of the tournament. He was booked on four criminal counts, including assault of a police officer, criminal mischief, reckless driving and disregarding signals from officers directing traffic.A police report obtained by Scripps News says he attempted to drive around traffic that was caused by a fatal accident near the country club. The report says Scheffler "refused to comply" with an officer directing traffic and "accelerated forward, dragging Detective Gillis to the ground."The officer was reportedly transported to a nearby hospital to be examined for "pain, swelling and abrasions to his left wrist and knee."Surveillance footage released by Louisville police last week appeared to show Gillis approaching Scheffler's vehicle on foot before stopping him from entering the golf course. Scheffler can later be seen being led away in handcuffs.In a statement released by the PGA Tour following his arrest, Scheffler described the incident as a "big misunderstanding.""I was proceeding as directed by police officers," he said. I never intended to disregard any of the instructions."Louisville police said last week they were looking into whether officers violated any department policies during the arrest. Gillis has since been disciplined for not having his body camera activated at the time of the incident.

Health authorities in France are sounding the alarm as cases of dengue continue to rise ahead of the 2024 Olympic Games.Officials say that this year alone there have been about “1,649 imported cases,” compared to about 131 cases reported around the same time last year, according to Euronews.The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says that the bulk of these cases stem from Guadeloupe and Martinique, where an "epidemic" is currently underway, as French Guiana has reported 7,000 confirmed dengue cases since the beginning of 2024.Officials are concerned because the Paris 2024 Olympic Games are only a few months away and scheduled to start on July 26, 2024.However, the French are not the only ones affected. This year, over 5 million cases have been reported worldwide that have resulted in 2,000 deaths, the ECDPC reports.The World Health Organization says that most of these cases are coming from the Americas, with Brazil, Argentina and Puerto Rico leading in cases.In March, Puerto Rico declared a public health emergency as the island reported 549 cases, nearly half of the total for the entire year of 2023 (1,242 cases). As of its latest data from April, the number had risen to 795.Dengue is a disease spread by mosquito bites, and symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pains, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands, rash, difficulty breathing, fatigue, and eye pain. If you have any of these symptoms, officials say to contact your primary care physician.

Yes, the Florida Panthers are already seeing injuries piling up.And yes, the Panthers know things could be much, much worse.Florida forward Brad Marchand will need six weeks to recover from his left leg injury and should be able to resume play with the Panthers sometime in November, coach Paul Maurice confirmed Friday. That comes on the heels of forward Aleksander Barkov, who is expected to need a similar timetable before he can play again, also because of a left leg injury.Losing two stars isn't good. But Maurice sees the silver lining."Nobody said 'months' yet," Maurice said.That's the difference between the injuries this season and what was happening to Florida at this point last season. By then, Barkov was already expected to be sidelined at least seven months with torn ligaments in his right knee and Matthew Tkachuk was also going to be out for multiple months while recovering from surgery to repair a sports hernia and torn adductor.Barkov wound up missing the entire season. Tkachuk didn't start his season until mid-January. The Panthers saw players miss a combined 544 games with injuries last season and missed the playoffs, an unceremonious end to their run as back-to-back Stanley Cup champions.So, yes, losing Barkov (who could be back by the end of November) and Marchand (who'll be back on the ice in three weeks, then is expected to need three more weeks to rehab and condition) for a few weeks now isn't ideal. But Florida has been there before."We're no stranger to guys going down the last few years and guys have done a great job of stepping up," Tkachuk said. "Worst case, you just got to win 1-0, 2-1."There have been clear sighs of relief with the knowledge that Barkov and Marchand will both return in a few weeks. Florida was short-handed in all four games of its season-opening road trip — Marchand missed the first two, Barkov missed the next two, and defenseman Aaron Ekblad also missed two because he and his wife were welcoming a baby — and the Panthers went 2-0-2 anyway.Ekblad is expected to be in the lineup when Florida plays its home opener Saturday against Minnesota."There's a threshold to this," Maurice said. "You can only survive so many (injuries) and we proved that. But you get two or three guys out, it's standard operating procedure in the National Hockey League. You prefer it's not your No. 1 at any one position because those guys hurt to lose. Everybody's got two or three. And then, you know, you get to five, it starts to get a little tight. Anything over five, you start to really feel it."

West Palm Beach native Markus Edegran is ready and hopeful to compete in his first Olympics.Markus will be competing in kite foiling. This combines kite boarding and foiling. Foiling is the latest technique to come into sailing.A foil is a type of board with an extended rudder. This allows the board to rise above the water and the sailor to move at much faster paces without the friction of the water along the board.When you achieve foiling, it is almost like you are flying over the water. Although it looks serene and peaceful, it is very difficult to achieve.Markus told us that it takes a lot of patience and balance to maintain the necessary foiling technique. He also explained that kite foiling goes at extreme paces, about 50 mph across the waters. He explained it best when he said that he can kite foil from Lake Worth Beach to the Juno Beach Pier faster than we can drive it.Markus explained to us what foiling means for the sport of sailing."The foiling is the way the sport is heading," Markus said. It's more exciting to sail. It's more exciting to watch. I think that half the classes are foiling classes. So yeah, super excited to be a part of that."He had an early introduction to the water as he followed his brothers’ footsteps and started sailing at 8 years old. He said there was a steep learning curve, but he was automatically hooked.I asked him about his emotions ahead of the games and he didn’t have much to say regarding those. Markus is very calm ahead of the games and is treating it just like any other five-day race."I'm super happy it all lined up and brought me here today," Markus said.He has been training in the Marseille waters off and on for the last three years ahead of the games. We are rooting for you Markus and hope you contribute to the USA medal count.Markus’ competition begins on Aug.

Boca Raton native Caroline Marks from the United States won the women's surfing gold medal on Monday at the Paris Olympics in Tahiti, while French Polynesian Kauli Vaast won the gold medal in men’s surfing.Marks, 22, was born in Boca but grew up in Melbourne Beach in Brevard County.SPECIAL COVERAGE: 2024 Paris OlympicsCheers and tears erupted from boats floating near the wave and crowds of spectators along the shore as the men's final match ended in the afternoon. Vaast pumped his arms into the air in victory after beating Jack Robinson from Australia, who received the silver medal.“I don’t really realize it, but I just made history,” said Vaast. “I can’t be prouder to represent Tahiti and France at home.”The women's gold medal match ended about thirty minutes later, with Marks beating Tatiana Weston-Webb from Brazil, who was awarded the silver medal.“Your whole life goes into a moment like this,” Marks said with a gold medal hanging around her neck. “It’s beyond all my wildest dreams.”For the bronze medals, Gabriel Medina from Brazil and Johanne Defay from France won after beating Alonso Correa from Peru and Brisa Hennessy from Costa Rica, respectively.“Chopes gave me so many good waves, so many good results. So I can’t complain,” said Medina, using a common nickname for Teahupo'o.Medalists — some in bare feet — stepped on to the Olympic podium near the ocean as crowds gathered to cheer and take photographs. Roosters ran along the grass while young local surfers called the names of the athletes as they walked by.All winners of the Paris Olympics surfing competition are first-time Olympic medalists, after defending Olympic women’s champion Carissa Moore of the United States — who won at the Tokyo Games, where Olympic surfing debuted — was beaten in the quarterfinals on Thursday.“Obviously I’m really sad to not be a part of finals day, to get to represent my home and my family one more time, but I’m really grateful,” Moore said after her loss. “I just hope that at the end of the day I can encourage whoever is watching, win or lose, don’t be afraid to go into it fearlessly and don’t be afraid to fail.”The final day of the Paris Olympics surfing competition began Monday morning after two days of delays due to unfavorable conditions. In the morning, conditions were smaller than the heavy, barrel-shaped waves Teahupo’o is famed for and that were seen during part of the men’s competition the week before.But by the afternoon waves grew larger and more frequent, giving athletes a chance to impress judges with the time they spent inside the barrels. At one point during the competition a whale jumped out of the water while surfers went head to head.Six of the eight surfers who made it to the semifinals represented different nations. French Polynesian, Peruvian, Australian and other national flags flew from boats near the waves.While not every surfer who competed was able to bring home a medal, many agreed that the second-ever Olympics surfing competition — filled with viral photographs, record-breaking scores and hours of stunning video footage broadcast to viewers around the world — helped promote the sport."Everyone’s watching and paying attention,” said Medina, who said he gained millions of social media followers after a photo of him floating in the sky next to his surfboard while bailing out of a wave went viral during the competition.

Rapper Pitbull has scored the naming rights to Florida International University’s football stadium in a new partnership with the Miami school.As part of a 10-year agreement, the university’s FIU Stadium will be rebranded as Pitbull Stadium, making it the first athletics stadium to be named after an artistPitbull, also known as “Mr. 305” for his Miami roots, will donate $1.2 million each year for the next five years as part of the deal.In addition to naming rights, Pitbull will be able to host up to 10 events a year, including concerts, at Pitbull Stadium. The school’s online store also has FIU x Pitbull merchandise available for purchase.The rapper, known for hits like "I Know You Want Me (Calle Ocho)," spoke out about the announcement."This partnership with FIU is a true honor and a testament to what we can achieve when we work hard," the music artist said in a press release. "Renaming the stadium isn't just about a name change. It's about inspiring the community, creating opportunities and showing the world that with determination and a clear vision, anything is possible. We're making history together, and we're just getting started. Why dream when you can live it?"FIU’s athletics director Scott Carr also commented on the partnership with the rapper, whose full name is Armando Christian Perez."This is a historic day for FIU Athletics to uniquely partner with a world-renowned artist and amazing person who truly values relationships and his community," Carr said in a press release. "Armando's financial support is program-changing, but him providing a microphone to amplify FIU will be even more beneficial to growing our brand. I couldn't be more excited about our partnership as this will take us to another level. We can now officially say: 'Paws Up, Dale!'"Van Wagner College, a third-party multimedia rights partner with FIU Athletics since 2016, assisted in the deal. The school helped secure additional partners, such as South Dade Kia, which FIU said will be the presenting sponsor of the field — South Dade Kia Field at Pitbull Stadium.No stranger to the education space, Pitbull also founded the first tuition-free public charter SLAM! school — for sports leadership, arts and management — in Miami in 2012.
