France’s high-speed rail network was hit Friday with widespread and “criminal” acts of vandalism including arson attacks, paralyzing travel to Paris from across the rest of France and Europe only hours before the grand opening ceremony of the Olympics.French officials condemned the attacks as “criminal actions,” though they said there was no sign of a direct link to the Games, and prosecutors in Paris opened a national investigation saying the crimes could carry sentences of 15 to 20 years.As Paris authorities geared up for a spectacular parade on and along the Seine River, three fires were reported near the tracks on the high-speed lines of Atlantique, Nord and Est, causing disruptions that affected hundreds of thousands of travelers.Among them were two German athletes in showjumping who were on a train to Paris to take part in the opening ceremony but had to turn back in Belgium because of the closures, and will now miss the ceremony, German news agency dpa reported.“There was no longer a chance of making it on time,” rider Philipp Weishaupt, who was traveling with teammate Christian Kukuk, told dpa.French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal wrote on the social media platform X that France’s intelligence services have been mobilized to find the perpetrators.Attal characterized them as “acts of sabotage,” which were “prepared and coordinated.”There were no known reports of injuries.RELATED STORY | Previewing the Paris Summer Olympics: When does it start, how to watchTransport Minister Patrice Vergriete described people fleeing from the scene of fires and the discovery of incendiary devices. “Everything indicates that these are criminal fires,” he said.The incidents paralyzed several high-speed lines linking Paris to the rest of France and to neighboring countries, Vergriete said, speaking on BFM television.The French national rail company SNCF said that areas affecting rail track intersections were targeted to double the impact.“For one fire, two destinations were hit,” the company's CEO, Jean-Pierre Farandou.It was “a premeditated, calculated, coordinated attack" that indicates "a desire to seriously harm” the French people, Farandou said.The attack occurred against a backdrop of global tensions and heightened security measures as the city prepared for the 2024 Olympic Games. Many travelers were planning to converge on the capital for the opening ceremony, and many vacationers were also in transit.French authorities have foiled several plots to disrupt the Olympics, including arresting a Russian man on suspicion of planning to destabilize the games.The Paris police prefecture “concentrated its personnel in Parisian train stations” after the “massive attack” that paralyzed the TGV high-speed network, Laurent Nuñez, the Paris police chief, told France Info television.RELATED STORY | Olympic soccer gets off to violent and chaotic start as Morocco fans rush the field vs ArgentinaAlso Friday, the French airport of Basel-Mulhouse on the border with Germany and Switzerland was evacuated in the morning and remained temporarily closed “for safety reasons," the airport said. It wasn't clear whether there was a connection to the rail attacks.The disruptions hit Paris’ Montparnasse station particular hard.In the station's crowded hall, Maiwenn Labbé-Sorin said she spent hours stranded on a train before it doubled back to Paris.“We stayed two hours without water, without toilets, without electricity," she said. "Then we could go out on the track for a bit and then the train returned. Now I’m not sure what’s going to happen.”Many passengers at the Gare du Nord, one of Europe’s busiest train stations, were looking for answers and solutions on Friday morning. All eyes were on the central message boards as most services to northern France, Belgium and the United Kingdom were delayed.“It’s a hell of a way to start the Olympics,” said Sarah Moseley, 42, as she learned that her train to London was an hour late.“They should have more information for tourists, especially if it’s a malicious attack,” said Corey Grainger, a 37-year-old Australian sales manager on his way to London, as he rested on his two suitcases in the middle of the station.Sports Minister Amélie Oudéa-Castera said authorities were working to “evaluate the impact on travelers, athletes, and ensure the transport of all delegations to the competition sites” for the Olympics. Speaking on BFM television, she added, “Playing against the Games is playing against France, against your own camp, against your country.”SNCF said it did not know when traffic would resume and feared that disruptions would continue “at least all weekend.” SNCF teams “were already on site to carry out diagnostics and begin repairs,” but the “situation should last at least all weekend while the repairs are carried out,” the operator said. SNCF advised “all passengers to postpone their journey and not to go to the station,” specifying in its press release that all tickets were exchangeable and refundable.Valerie Pecresse, president of the regional council of the greater Paris region, speaking from Montparnasse station, said “250,000 travelers will be affected today on all these lines.” Substitution plans were underway, but Pecresse advised travelers “not to go to stations.”The troubles comes ahead of an opening ceremony has been planned for later Friday, in which 7,000 Olympic athletes are due to sail down the Seine past iconic Parisian monuments such as Notre-Dame Cathedral, the Louvre Museum, and the Musee d’Orsay.

Celebrating its reputation as a cradle of revolution, Paris kicked off its first Summer Olympics in a century on Friday with a rain-soaked, rule-breaking opening ceremony studded with stars and fantasy along the Seine River.On-and-off showers — the first rain at a Summer Olympics' opening ceremony in more than 70 years — did not seem to hamper the enthusiasm of the athletes. Some held umbrellas as they rode boats down the river in a showcase of the city’s resilience as authorities investigated suspected acts of sabotage targeting France's high-speed rail network.Widespread travel disruptions triggered by what French officials called coordinated arson attacks on high-speed rail lines as well as the weather had dampened the mood ahead of the ceremony.Still, crowds crammed the Seine's banks and bridges and watched from balconies, “oohing” and “aahing” as Olympic teams paraded in boats down the waterway that got increasingly choppy as the weather worsened.Undeterred from the festivities, many of the hundreds of thousands of spectators huddled under umbrellas, plastic ponchos or jackets as the rain intensified, others danced and sang, and some dashed from their seats for shelter.“The rain can't stop us,” said U.S. basketball star LeBron James, sporting a plastic poncho along with the other American flag bearer, tennis player Coco Gauff.The weather made for some bizarre scenes at the show combining prerecorded and live performances: a stiff upper-lipped pianist played on even as small puddles formed on his grand piano. A breakdancer flipped her moves on the sheen of a rain-drenched platform. Some athletes in Bermuda-style colorful shirts looked dressed for the beach, not a deluge.As global audiences tuned in, Paris put its best foot forward — quite literally, with a spectacular Olympic launch that lifted spirits and joyous French cancan dancers featured early on. A humorous short film featured soccer icon Zinedine Zidane. Plumes of French blue, white and red smoke followed.Lady Gaga sang in a prerecorded performance, in French, with dancers shaking pink plumed pompoms, injecting a cabaret feel. To close the show, Celine Dion, standing under the Eiffel Tower, belted out her first live performance since the French-Canadian singer was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder, at the end of 2022.French-Malian pop star Aya Nakamura, the most listened-to French-speaking artist in the world, emerged from a pyrotechnic display in an all-gold out to sing her hit “Djadja” accompanied by a Republican guard band of the French army.More than three hours into the show, French President Emmanuel Macron declared the Games open. In a gaffe shortly beforehand, the five-ring Olympic flag was raised upside down at the Trocadero across from the Eiffel Tower.The final torch relay spanned landmarks like the Louvre and included sports legends like tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal before French judo champ Teddy Riner and three-time Olympic champion runner Marie-Jose Perec lit the Olympic cauldron attached to a giant balloon, which floated into the Paris night.The ceremony celebrated women, including 10 golden statues of female pioneers that rose from giant pedestals along the river. Among them was Olympe de Gouges, who drafted the Declaration of the Rights of Women and the Female Citizen in 1791 during the French Revolution. She campaigned for the abolition of slavery and was guillotined in 1793.The Paris Games aim to be the first with equal numbers of men and women competing.With the ambitious ceremony, the stakes for France were immense. Dozens of heads of state and government were in town, and the world was watching as Paris turned itself into a giant open-air theater. Along the Seine, iconic monuments became stages for dancers, singers and other artists.Sofia Cohen, 20, watching with her father, called the ceremony “electric.” The Nicaraguan-Americans said the roar of applause given to the Ukrainian team was their favorite part.“Every Olympics is different, and this one was very French. The ceremony started out very majestic and regal. And as the rain started pouring down and time went on, everything got a little more hectic and fun,” she said.The sprawling event gave organizers bigger crowds to transport, organize and safeguard than would have been the case if they’d followed the example of previous Olympic host cities that opened with stadium shows.Still, as the show got underway, optimism soared that Paris — true to its motto that speaks of being unsinkable — might just see its gambles pay off. That's despite the soggy weather — no other Summer Olympics opening ceremony has had rain since Helsinki in 1952.Paris organizers said 6,800 of the 10,500 athletes would attend before they embark on the next 16 days of competition.The boats carrying the Olympic teams started the parade by breaking through curtains of water that cascaded down from Austerlitz Bridge, the start of the 6-kilometer (nearly 4-mile) route. The jetting waters were a wink at the fountains of Versailles Palace, the venue for Olympic equestrian competitions.Per Olympic protocol, the first boat carried athletes from Greece, birthplace of the ancient Games. It was followed by the Olympic team of refugee athletes and then, the other nations in French alphabetical order.Usually during Olympic opening ceremonies, the parade of athletes takes place during a pause in the razzmatazz. But Paris shattered that tradition by having the parade and pageantry at the same time, blending sports and artistic expression.Some spectators who followed organizers’ advice to arrive well ahead of time along the ceremony route fumed over long waits to get to their seats.“Paris has been great, anything to do with the Olympics and dissemination of information has been horrible,” said Tony Gawne, a 54-year-old Texan who turned up six hours in advance with his wife.“When you spend $6,000 on two tickets, well, that’s a little frustrating,” he said.But Paris had plenty of aces up its sleeve. The Eiffel Tower, its head visible below the clouds, Notre Dame Cathedral — restored from the ashes of its 2019 fire — the Louvre Museum and other iconic monuments starred in the opening ceremony. Award-winning theater director Thomas Jolly, the show’s creative mind, was using the signature Paris cityscape of zinc-gray rooftops as the playground for his imagination.His task: Tell the story of France, its people, their history and essence in a way that leaves an indelible imprint on Olympic audiences. Refresh the image and self-confidence of the French capital that was repeatedly struck by deadly extremist attacks in 2015. Capture how Paris is also aiming to reboot the Olympics, with Summer Games it has worked to make more appealing and sustainable.It’s a big ask. So Paris went big, very big. That goes for the security, too. Large fenced-off stretches of central Paris were locked down to those without passes and the skies during the ceremony were a no-fly zone for 93 miles around.During the athletes’ waterborne adventure, they passed historic landmarks that have been temporarily transformed into arenas for Olympic sports.Concorde Plaza, where French revolutionaries guillotined King Louis XVI and other royals, now hosting skateboarding and other sports. The golden-domed resting place of Napoléon Bonaparte, the backdrop for Olympic archery, and the Eiffel Tower, which donated chunks of iron that have been inlaid in the gold, silver and bronze Olympic medals. They’ll be won in the 32 sports’ 329 medal events.Paris’ aim, said Estanguet, is “to show to the whole world and to all of the French that in this country, we’re capable of exceptional things.”

A hot topic amongst tourists and athletes at the 2024 Olympics is the decision France made to forgo including air conditioning in Olympic Village.Some countries have chosen to supply their own air conditioning units to their competitors, like Team USA. Other countries have agreed with France's decision and will not provide air conditioning to their athletes.Summertime in Paris is much more tolerable than you initially would think.The average high temperatures are in the mid 70s with overnight lows in the upper 50s and low 60s.Last year, Paris did deal with record-breaking heat as temperatures soared over 86 degrees.A key component to keeping the Olympic Village between 73 and 79 degrees is in the piping. Water pipes under the floor's surface will aid in keeping the village in more comfortable conditions without the aid of air conditioning units.This is all in an effort to make the 2024 Olympics the greenest yet.France has kept the goal of keeping carbon emissions at a minimum this year. You will notice most of the Olympic sporting venues are historic sites where they only had to construct grandstands and the competition ground, rather than building new Olympic structures.

Salt Lake City has officially been named the host city for the 2034 Winter Olympics.International Olympic Committee President Thomas Bach made the announcement during a livestreamed session Wednesday from Paris, where the Summer Olympics are gearing up.“The International Olympic Committee has the honor to announce that the 27th Winter Games 2034 are awarded to Salt Lake City, Utah,” Bach said.RELATED STORY | Previewing the Paris Summer Olympics: When does it start, how to watchCheers and applause erupted in the crowd, with a number of Utah officials in attendance.Salt Lake City previously hosted the Winter Olympics back in 2002, and its sports venues from then still exist.Utah Gov. Spencer Cox took the podium following the news, and thanked the IOC for its generosity.RELATED STORY | Coco Gauff named Team USA's youngest-ever flag bearer, joins Lebron James“Our commitment to you is that we will work to unify, not just the United States of America, but the entire world around sports again,” Cox said. “Our world needs the Olympic and Paralympic movement now more than ever, and we will make you proud.”“To the people celebrating back home — we're back, baby,” Cox said.The IOC also approved a bid for the French Alps to host the 2030 Winter Games on Wednesday, but that is tentative. There are conditions attached to the approval and whoever becomes the next prime minister of France will have to sign off on it.

A 17-year-old was killed in a shooting Friday night at Garcia's Boat Ramp in Indian River County, and investigators are examining whether the shooting was an act of self-defense, according to Sheriff Eric Flowers.WATCH: WPTV'S Coverage of Teen killed in Garcia's Boat Ramp shootingThe shooting happened during a confrontation at the popular waterfront gathering spot, which authorities say has become a frequent meetup location for teenagers.According to Flowers, investigators reviewed video that showed the 17-year-old opening the door of a truck and throwing punches at people inside before a shot was fired."The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch. He's going to punch the people that are inside of that truck," Flowers said during a news conference. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed the 17-year-old in this case."Video released by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office shows the confrontation moments before the shooting.Flowers said social media has played a role in drawing large groups of teens to locations like Garcia's Boat Ramp and warned that the presence of firearms is increasing the risks associated with those gatherings."We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," Flowers said. "Now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix, and so what we're seeing is an escalation of each one of these."Authorities said both the shooter and the driver of the truck have cooperated with investigators, turning over the firearm and the vehicle involved in the incident.As of Monday, no arrests had been made."It's gonna be up to the state on whether charges are ultimately filed, but I can tell you, self-defense plays a part in these," Flowers said.The investigation remains active. The sheriff is asking anyone with video footage or information about the shooting, as well as future teen meetup events, to contact investigators.Flowers also urged parents to know where their children are and suggested location-tracking tools as one way to help keep them safe.

Lake Worth Beach is reducing fines for bulk and vegetation pickup violations and issuing partial refunds to residents after public backlash over 12-hundred citations issued since August.The city said more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began Aug. 9 under its bulk trash and vegetation pickup rules. Residents complained they were unaware of the stricter enforcement and said they received costly citations without warning.The change comes after concerns raised by residents. Luis Carvajal, a Lake Worth Beach resident since 2009, contacted WPTV after receiving a bill that included a $335 violation charge.Carvajal said landscapers working on his property had trimmed palm fronds and placed them near the street for pickup."They're still continuing to work in the backyard or whatever. And there are trucks out here, and then the city solid waste comes by and they scoop it up and they leave. Okay, I didn't think nothing of it," Carvajal told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.Days later, he received a bill in the mail."Make it make sense to me. It didn't make sense," Carvajal said. "They're Palm Beach prices."Carvajal said he had never previously received a city violation notice.Concerns about the fines quickly spread among residents and eventually reached the Lake Worth Beach City Commission.According to city officials, though the changes went into effect in October 2025, more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began in August, generating widespread criticism from residents who said they were not adequately informed about the rules.Vice Mayor Mimi May acknowledged residents frustrations during recent commission discussions."As somebody who's sitting here all the time, I'm like, how do you not know that?" May said. "But if I was just a non-informed resident, I would be upset about that."May is one of the officials who helped spearhead the changes when the ordinance took effect in October 2025.At the time, she recommended fines as high as $500 and opposed sending notification letters to residents before enforcement began.Now, she has changed her position."$300 is way too much money for people on a fixed income," May said.The vice mayor also issued a public apology on social media."I sincerely apologize for any confusion or frustration this situation has caused. I understand that a $335 fine can be a significant financial burden, especially when someone may not have fully understood the rules," May wrote.City leaders have now approved changes to the penalty structure.The city has reduced the violation fine from $335 to $135. Officials also plan to reimburse affected residents $200 for each violation issued under the previous rate.For residents like Carvajal, the city's decision comes as welcome news."That's great news, and I thank Channel 5 for looking into this matter," he told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.City officials say the reduced fines are now in effect, and eligible residents will receive reimbursements related to previous violations on their next bill.

Five years after Gabriella "Gabi" Hanley was shot and killed in an apparent drive-by shooting in Port St. Lucie, no arrests have been made in her case.WATCH BELOW: Family seeks answers 5 years after loved one killedHanley, 20, was shot along Green River Parkway in 2021. Her boyfriend, who was in the car at the time, was also hit by gunfire but survived. Hanley left behind a 14-month-old daughter, who is now 6 years old.Port St. Lucie police identified several people of interest at the time of the shooting, but five years later, no one has been arrested.The pain of losing Gabi still lingers for her mother, Nicole Vigilante."It is tough, but I gotta be strong for my granddaughter," Vigilante said.As Gabi's daughter grows older, the family is searching for answers — for themselves and for her."Now she's getting older, and she has questions," Vigilante said. "And we want to be able to give her those answers," Krystal Benitez, Gabi's cousin, added.For Gabi's loved ones, her daughter is a constant reminder of who she was."We're reminded of the situation every single day," Alexia Perez, Gabi's best friend, said. "We will never forget Gabi. Her daughter is walking memory of her.""Gabi was an amazing, amazing woman," Benitez added.Port St. Lucie police turned to social media Tuesday, saying information that was not shared at the time of the shooting could make a difference today. They're asking anyone with information to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department's Major Crimes Division at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477.Gabi's family and friends are doing their part to keep the case alive by sharing her story and raising awareness throughout the community."We have been spending the day handing out flyers going to all local businesses just trying to again raise awareness," Benitez said.They are now calling on the community to come forward with information."There's a little girl right now that's being raised without her mother, so be brave for her and come forward," Benitez said.Read more of WPTV's related stories:Port St. Lucie police identify 3 persons of interest in fatal shooting of Gabriella HanleyMystery gunman fires shots into car in Port St. Lucie, killing womanThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Five years have passed, but the shooting death of 20-year-old Gabriella Hanley remains unsolved. No one has been charged with her death, and Port St. Lucie police are asking anyone with information to come forward.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie police investigating deadly shootingOn Oct. 5, 2021, at around 11:45 p.m., Port St. Lucie police said they responded to reports of multiple gunshots near Southeast Green River Parkway and Southeast Charleston Drive.Hanley was driving southbound on Southeast Green River Parkway in a black Kia Forte with her boyfriend, 21-year-old Darrick Mincey Jr., when another vehicle pulled alongside them and fired multiple rounds into their car, police said.Hanley was shot multiple times, police said. Officers and rescue personnel immediately attempted lifesaving measures, but she later died in the early morning hours on Oct. Mincey was also struck by gunfire but survived.Investigators said they determined the Kia sustained 37 bullet impacts during the shooting. Numerous 9mm cartridge casings were recovered from the scene, and subsequent forensic examination determined they had been fired from two different firearms, police said.The suspect vehicle was described as a silver four-door sedan that fled southbound on Southeast Green River Parkway.In the years since Hanley's death, Port St. Lucie Police Department detectives have continued to investigate her death, conducting numerous interviews, examining forensic and digital evidence, and following up on investigative leads.As of Tuesday, no one has been charged with Hanley's death, and police continue to search for answers.If you know something about what happened to Hanley that night, no matter how insignificant you may think it is, Port St. Lucie police are asking you to come forward. Lucie Police Department – Major Crimes Division at 772-871-5000 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS (8477). A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.WATCH BELOW: Student critically injured after being struck by SUVInvestigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on his way to school and was near the edge of the roadway alongside construction barrels in the area when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.According to police, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. Authorities said the driver later made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene.Once back in the area, the driver activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation.The student suffered life-threatening injuries and remains hospitalized in critical condition, according to police.Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The crash remains under investigation.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the crash to come forward.Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.Howard Shapiro lives across the street from where the crash occurred.Shapiro said this stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard can be dangerous."I don't walk around here is no lighting outside at nighttime," said Shapiro. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there."Though crews are improving the roadway, Shapiro said lights would make it safer."They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's going to be helpful. But streetlights need to follow," said Shapiro.Celine Gabriel lives off nearby Becker Road and said she avoids Port St. Lucie Boulevard altogether."I don't even come down this road no more," said Gabriel. "I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's “not exactly his favorite senator.”Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. Trump lost the state in 2024, giving Democrats hope of defeating the five-term moderate Republican, who has been targeted by Democrats in previous elections and survived.RELATED STORY | Senate Republicans move cash from purple North Carolina to red Kansas as battle for majority shiftsDuring the hourlong debate, Jackson focused largely on attempting to connect Collins to Trump. He kicked off the night by pointing out she cast a critical vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump nominee who eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion. Collins supports abortion rights and said Kavanaugh assured her it was settled law, but she has said recently that she does not regret her vote to confirm him.“Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?” asked Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger.He also repeatedly brought up her procedural vote to advance the president’s 2025 tax and spending bill — though Collins ultimately broke with her party to vote against it.Collins countered that she has voted against Trump more than she did Joe Biden when the Democrat was president, and has pushed back against Trump on tariffs, immigration enforcement and the war in Iran.“I voted against my party more than another other senator on either side of the aisle,” Collins said.The attention on Trump comes as only 31% of U.S. adults approved of how the Republican is handling the presidency, according to a September AP-NORC poll. That’s well below where his approval stood when he took office last year.The president has started holding rallies around the country in an effort to help GOP candidates win in November, telling voters to pretend he is on the ballot. At Tuesday's debate, a moderator noted Trump has floated the idea of campaigning in Maine, and asked Collins if she would stand beside him if he does.RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour“I’m not exactly his favorite senator,” she said, adding “I would say that he’s not coming to Maine.”Collins, who has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: “Leadership matters in Washington.”She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine’s high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing “Augusta’s failed policies” as a way to connect Jackson’s to the state’s struggle to address affordability.Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. For example, as Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”Jackson and Collins are scheduled to participate in three more debates later this month.

With less than a month until Election Day, Democrats are looking beyond the traditional battlegrounds as new signs emerge that the fight for control of Congress could be spreading into states Republicans once had little reason to worry about. Kansas and Florida are among the states receiving new attention, while President Donald Trump’s own campaign schedule is taking him into reliably Republican territory. RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tourThe shift can also be seen in campaign spending. Conservative groups have recently moved money from North Carolina, where the Senate contest was expected to be one of the year’s most competitive races, to Kansas as Democrats perform better in both states. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. “Since Labor Day, the numbers have only gotten worse for Republicans,” said Kyle Kondik, a nonpartisan election analyst with the University of Virginia Center for Politics. Florida is another state to watch. Democrats are increasingly campaigning there even though the state appeared on relatively few lists of major battlegrounds earlier this year. RELATED STORY | Trump takes midterm push to Nebraska amid economic concerns among farmersKondik said Florida could become an important early indicator on election night if Democrats are having an especially strong showing. “That’s a state that counts very quickly,” Kondik said. Trump, meanwhile, campaigned this week in Nebraska, a state he carried by nearly 200,000 votes two years ago. The president frequently calls polls fake, and Kondik cautioned that the current political picture could still be affected by inaccurate polling. “I am always concerned about there being some systematic polling error,” he said. Republicans currently hold 218 seats in the House, while the Senate has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats. Democrats need 51 Senate votes to hold a majority, while Republicans need 50 because the vice president breaks ties. The final weeks of the campaign will help determine whether the activity in Kansas, Florida and other states marks a genuine expansion of the political battlefield or whether the fight for Congress ultimately returns to more familiar battlegrounds.

Republicans are making an appeal to Hispanic voters in the final stretch of the midterm election, as Trump blitzes the country to boost his party.The president is expected to make a second stop in a matter of weeks to the border state of Texas Wednesday.It comes as the economy and immigration enforcement weigh on some Hispanic voters, but republicans maintain confidence in support.“I loved you for many years before I ever decided to do this political thing, and you liked me from the beginning because the numbers are incredible, and I appreciate it,” Trump said during a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration at the White House last week.RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tourRepublicans are urging Hispanic voters, as they are Trump’s supporters broadly, to turn out on Election Day, pointing to job growth, investments and tax cuts under the Trump administration.“Sit this election out, and you could be left with socialist senators in Texas and Florida, and a government that looks less like the America your family helped build, and more like the communist dictatorships many Hispanic Americans fled,” approval.More than two thirds of Latino voters disapprove of President Trump, according to a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll, which also found nearly a fifth who supported Trump in 2024 don’t prefer a Research Center survey in April found of Hispanic voters that supported Trump in 2024, 66 percent approved of the job he was doing, a drop of more than 20 percent from the start of the term and a for Hispanic voters.“We have talked to several Trump voters on the ground, Latino Trump voters, who, because the economy is so bad, because they feel like Trump hasn't focused on any of the priorities he said he was going to focus on. President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state.But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.“You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our country.”The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”Texas has become an unexpected battleground for RepublicansThe Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.RELATED STORY | Obama is set to get more involved in the midterms, starting with an appearance alongside Abdul El-SayedIn a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primaryWhile the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. “He’s a fantastic man.”Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution.Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here."Trump makes a big announcement, but not about the Senate raceWhile Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame.Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.”

A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the party’s future, in one of the party’s first major gatherings following the election.Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. A deadly school bus crash in Polk County is raising new questions about how students are protected inside Florida school buses and why state law still falls short of federal safety recommendations.One student, a 10th grader on her way to Winter Haven High School, was killed Monday morning when a school bus carrying 39 people was involved in a crash. The circumstances surrounding the crash remain under investigation, including what happened outside the bus and what took place inside it.Watch report from Katie Lagrone"We have one fatality of a beautiful high school girl. It's just heartbreaking," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a morning news briefing.Investigators have not released details about how many students were wearing seat belts, what type of restraints were in use, or whether the belts played a role in the outcome of the crash.Florida law requires school buses built since 2001 to be equipped with seat belts. However, students are not required to wear them, and state law does not require the more protective lap-and-shoulder belts recommended by federal safety investigators. Instead, many Florida school buses continue to use standard lap belts.The federal recommendation followed an investigation by investigative reporter Katie LaGrone more than a decade ago.In 2012, a St. Lucie County school bus collided with a semi-truck, killing 9-year-old Aaron Beauchamp. Aaron was wearing the bus's standard lap belt at the time of the crash.Several years later, investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) examined that crash and studied how different types of seat belts affect student safety.The agency's testing showed significant differences between standard lap belts and lap-and-shoulder restraints. Simulations demonstrated that lap-and-shoulder belts provide greater protection by better controlling a passenger's movement during a crash.As a result, the NTSB recommended that all school buses nationwide be equipped with lap-and-shoulder belts.The NTSB specifically urged Florida to change state law to require lap-and-shoulder belts on new large school buses.That recommendation was never adopted.Today, it remains unclear how many Florida school districts have voluntarily upgraded their fleets to meet the federal recommendation.In St. Lucie County, nearly 15 years after Aaron's death, about 20% of district school buses still use only standard lap belts.In Polk County, a district spokesperson confirmed on Monday that all the district’s school buses are equipped with just lap belts.The latest crash has renewed questions about whether stronger seat belt requirements could better protect students who are traveling to and from school on a school bus.Despite the concerns raised by this tragedy, transportation safety experts continue to emphasize that deadly school bus crashes are extremely rare, and that school buses remain the safest form of transportation for students traveling to and from school.For families in Polk County and across Florida, the crash could prompt renewed scrutiny of whether the state's school bus safety standards should be updated to reflect federal recommendations."No one will ever understand how heavy this weighs on our hearts," Polk County Schools Superintendent Fred Heid said following the crash.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. A Martin County employee is being praised for her quick actions after rescuing a girl from drowning at Bob Graham Beach in Stuart on Thursday afternoon. Amy Offenbach, who came to the beach to surf, said the day took an unexpected turn. "It was just by chance that we were here and thank God that we were at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts kicked in when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water, and the beach had no lifeguards on duty. Offenbach rushed in to help, using a surfboard to stabilize the girl. "Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. Offenbach said the girl's forehead felt cold, prompting her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries. "I'm just really thankful that her parents have their child," Offenbach said. Offenbach, a Martin County employee, said she doesn’t feel the need for recognition. While some are calling her a hero, Offenbach said she was simply acting on her instincts as a mother. "I have a 14-year-old son myself, and I can't imagine him not coming back from hanging out at the beach with his friends," she said. The incident serves as a reminder to exercise caution at the beach, especially in areas without lifeguards. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

Martin County's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders.Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," Martin County officials said in the statement.Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, "we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.”Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown."We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system," Martin County Transit said.In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county.Jim Gordon, Martin County's Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming."We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today," Gordon said.For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily."[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food," Joe said.Joe said he received no notice before service was cut."No warning at all, nothing, zero." Joe said.Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere," Joe said.Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company's handling of the shutdown lacked transparency."I don't think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it," Houwaart-Diez said.Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption."This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor's, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there," Houwaart-Diez said.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program's response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. "Growing up here, I'm a sixth-generation pioneer, so that really means something here. Grew up here, went to school here, currently raising my family, and now I'm here serving the community that I know and love."While Jupiter's new stations, apparatus and equipment are central to the launch, Donatto said the department's personnel are what make the milestone meaningful."The most exciting thing is the people in it," Donatto said. "We've just been so incredibly blessed to hire some of the best people in the world. They're excited to serve the town of Jupiter."By 5 a.m. Thursday, Jupiter Fire Rescue's firefighters and paramedics had already answered four calls while introducing the community to the people and equipment behind the new department.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductibles," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone. Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it. During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

The WPTV Town Hall on Amendment 3 has led to more questions about the referendum facing voters on raising the homestead exemption to lower property taxes and reduce revenue for cities and counties.One question attendees posed was: Why are our property taxes increasing every year?WATCH BELOW: Florida property tax increases explained ahead of Amendment 3 votePalm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo talked about it at the town hall, saying inflation is a big factor."This is a national problem, not even a Florida problem; it's not a Palm Beach County problem," Abruzzo said.
