Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

MARTY public transit service in Martin County came to an abrupt halt Thursday, leaving residents who depend on the transit system without regular transportation as county officials scramble to find a solution. Martin County officials told WPBF's Caleb Califano they were given no advance warning that service would stop Thursday. According to the county, MARTY’s operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract. The company says rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs have led to significant financial losses since it began operating the service in July 2025. Despite negotiations with the county, the two sides were unable to reach an agreement. County officials said the company provided a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. However, Thursday morning, Martin County Transit LLC notified the county that it was immediately discontinuing service. The sudden shutdown has left residents who rely on MARTY to get around the county without their regular transportation option. George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said officials are now exploring both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It’s just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It’s going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." In the meantime, county officials say they are working with community partners, including United Way, to help residents impacted by the shutdown. The county has not provided a timeline for when MARTY operations could resume. Officials say they will continue posting updates on social media and will notify residents as soon as a solution is reached. For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.Now, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

Two women in Fort Pierce are accused of animal neglect after a dog died on their watch, according to arrest reports from the Fort Pierce Police Department . FPPD says that Samya Shanice Bryant, 25, and Danielle Amanda Potts, 28, were arrested on Oct. 2 in connection with the neglect and death of a dog at Pine Creek Apartments. Officers found the dog days before on Sept. 29 lying outside an apartment. The dog was severely underweight with visible ribs, infected sores on his paws, and no food or water. Bryant told the officers that the dog was hers, and that he had been sick for weeks after another man allegedly poured boiling water on him. FPPD says that both women who each lived in the apartment had control of the dog but did not get him veterinary treatment. See also: Trump touts West Palm golf club as possible Camp David-style retreat for future presidents Animal Control took the dog for emergency care, but the dog had to be euthanized on Oct. 2 because of injuries, infections and organ failure. Both Bryant and Potts were arrested and are being charged with aggravated animal cruelty and confining/impounding an animal without sufficient food or water.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest. “I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue,” Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. “That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast.” The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. “I think we’d be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don’t have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we’re at least prepared just in case these two firms aren’t available, non-responsive,” Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. “I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don’t want to delay any further.” The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30 , when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district’s own contract employees. “Since this district’s inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves,” Fowler said during that meeting. “They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves.” Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director. The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone. “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,” Hutchinson said. “We’re all still friends,” Boudrias said. “Us and the victims, there was no ill intent.” The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled. Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter. “That’s not a good process,” Fowler previously told WPTV. Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny. “I’m glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue,” Lee said, adding that he “welcomes any investigation from any agency.” Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a “sad day” and saying she had been a “tremendous attorney for the district.” Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee. “It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district,” Fowler previously said. “So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that’s a pretty impactful message.” Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote. “We’ll see what the men and women decide,” Lee said. “I came up on the labor side; I’ve always fought for our men and women on the line.” The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out. “I think we might actually,” Fowler said at the time. Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductible," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school Wednesday morning, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.WATCH BELOW: Student critically injured after being struck by SUVInvestigators said the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard on his way to school and was near the edge of the roadway alongside construction barrels in the area when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.According to police, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. Authorities said the driver later made a U-turn at the next location where it was safe to do so and returned to the scene.Once back in the area, the driver activated his hazard lights and found the teen unconscious on the side of the roadway. Police said he immediately called 911 and has remained cooperative throughout the investigation.The student suffered life-threatening injuries and remains hospitalized in critical condition, according to police.Investigators said there were no apparent signs of impairment involving the driver, though they noted the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The crash remains under investigation.Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have dash camera, surveillance or other video footage from the area around the time of the crash to come forward.Anyone with information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.Howard Shapiro lives across the street from where the crash occurred.Shapiro said this stretch of Port St. Lucie Boulevard can be dangerous."I don't walk around here is no lighting outside at nighttime," said Shapiro. "Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there."Though crews are improving the roadway, Shapiro said lights would make it safer."They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's going to be helpful. But streetlights need to follow," said Shapiro.Celine Gabriel lives off nearby Becker Road and said she avoids Port St. Lucie Boulevard altogether."I don't even come down this road no more," said Gabriel. "I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school.

A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

Martin County officials are scrambling to restore public transportation service after the county's contracted transit provider abruptly canceled its services, leaving Martin County Public Transit (MARTY) riders without transportation effective immediately. In a statement Thursday, Martin County said it is aware that its contracted transit service provider has canceled service and that MARTY transit operations are currently interrupted. "Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," the county said. "Additional information will be provided as it becomes available." Officials did not immediately identify the transit provider or explain why the service was canceled. "We understand the importance of MARTY services to our community and apologize for the disruption," the statement said. In response, United Way of Martin County said it is preparing for an increase in transportation assistance requests through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents. Region Martin County "Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table," said Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County. "When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it." United Way officials said the program was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption. The organization is now anticipating an even greater need for transportation assistance. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support Ride United's response to the outage. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. WPTV reached out to Martin County Transit who responded with this statement: "We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system." Martin County Transit told WPTV that 29 employees will be losing jobs as a result of the contract termination. Residents seeking transportation assistance can call 772-283-4800 or visit https://www.unitedwaymartin.org/rideunited for more information. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website .

After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find other accomedations if they can, whether that be another place to stay or carpooling in vehicles that can handle minor flooding. He also said that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems, and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said the work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, canal pumps, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design, and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-24 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from the $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment. That went into effect Oct. 1 and raised the assessment from $189 to $195. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

A 17-year-old boy died after a shooting late Friday close to a boat ramp near Fellsmere and Vero Beach, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Saturday. The Indian River School District said the unnamed teen recently withdrew from Sebastian River High School to homeschool and was not enrolled in the district at the time of the shooting. "We are deeply saddened by the loss of this young person, and our hearts are with his family, friends, and the Sebastian River High School community," district spokeswoman Kyra Schafte said in a statement to WPBF. In a follow-up email she wrote: "This remains an active investigation, and we are in constant communication with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Please direct questions about the investigation to IRCSO. Our primary focus is supporting our students, staff, families, and community during this difficult time." A dance is scheduled for 7 p.m. Saturday at Sebastian River High. Read more at: https://www.miamiherald.com/news/article317482082.html#storylink=cpy At 11:24 p.m., deputies responded to reports of a juvenile shot in the area of Garcia's Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512 and near the Fort Drum Marsh Conservation Area. Deputies located the teen and began lifesaving measures until Indian River County Fire Rescue arrived. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries, the sheriff's office said. "At this time, this appears to be an isolated incident, and there is no threat to the public," Lt. Kevin Jaworski wrote in an alert to the media. "This is an active investigation." He told WPBF that investigators have interviewed all parties involved in the case. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office (772-569-6700) or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers (1-800-273-TIPS). Detectives from the Criminal Investigations Division and crime scene personnel were processing the scene and interviewing multiple witnesses. The area remains open to the public. A woman fled for her life after she was attacked and later shot at as she drove away in her vehicle. According to the Fort Pierce Police Department , on Saturday, October 3, officers responded to South Sixth Street at 7:12 a.m. after the victim called police and reported that someone was shooting at her. The investigation revealed the victim went to South Sixth Street to speak with her boyfriend about their relationship. Upon her arrival, several people ran out of the residence and began attacking her. See also: Opponents, supporters clash over Palm Beach County Israel Bonds investments Police said the victim was able to escape, get into her vehicle, and drive away. As she fled, one of the suspects grabbed a gun from the property and began shooting at her, according to police. A second person was arrested for allegedly driving the shooter away from the scene. The two suspects arrested were identified as Keibin Lopez-Godoy, 18, and Kailee Yurubi, 18. Godoy faces a charge of first-degree attempted homicide. Yurubi faces a charge of accessory after the fact.

The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses.Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing."I would say it's about 25% higher need," she said.People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher."They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough," Mejia said. "So, that's why we're coming in and filling in the gap." The Soup Kitchen is filling in the gap for every walk of life, including employed residents, who have homes and cars but are still not making ends meet at the end of the month."You can see people from all over and we call them the household person, which is asset limited income constrained," Mejia said. "But they're employed, so they have cars, they may have a house, they may have an apartment, and it's just not adding up at the end of the month." Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food."I just come here. They have good food every day. So, I'm thank God I'm here," Marcellus said.The kitchen is able to distribute hundreds of pounds of food every day through faithful volunteers, like Mary Webb."You just feel good helping out other people and it comes back to you," Webb said. "The goodness comes back to you." The Soup Kitchen is located at 8655 W. and they can be contacted at 561-732-7595.

Heavy rain flooded roads across Port St. Lucie Tuesday afternoon, leaving some vehicles stranded, forcing children to walk through standing water after school and prompting a response from police officers and city crews. According to the City of Port St. Lucie , a large amount of rain fell in a short period of time, leading to temporary road closures and flooding in multiple areas. Public Works crews responded to flooding near Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, closing the roadway until it was safe for travel. The city also reported high-water conditions near Thornhill Drive and Floresta Drive, where Phase 3 construction is underway. On Southwest Thornhill Drive, school buses continued dropping off students despite flooded streets. CBS12 News saw children step off buses carrying their shoes and walk barefoot through standing water to reach home. Along Southwest Broadview Avenue near Crosstown Parkway, residents watched as water spilled across the roadway, making it difficult for drivers to tell where the street ended and floodwater began. "If you didn't see the grass here, you wouldn't know where the road is," resident Kevin Burke told CBS12 News. "It was steady sheets of rain for a good hour. Non-stop, and I mean heavy, heavy." Police officers directed traffic while Public Works crews set up barricades and monitored conditions during the evening commute. Burke said flooding in the area has become a familiar problem during heavy downpours. "When it rains heavy like it did today, it's like this all the time, from that canal coming up," he said. Burke said standing water presents concerns beyond traffic issues. "We have a pond over there by Crosstown and Bayshore. It's got signs all around it saying there are gators in it. It's a long shot, but it could happen, and that's what worries me, with kids and the animals," he said. For some residents, the flooding disrupted everyday tasks. "She has her elderly brother, who's 83 years old, and she's in her 60s, and she was going to run out and get Chinese food, and now she's still sitting here waiting because she can't get to it," Burke said. Earlier in the day, Port St. Lucie police reported flooding at several intersections, including SE Evans Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SE Eyerly Avenue and SE Airoso Boulevard, SW Bayshore Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, and NE Floresta Drive and NE Ardsley Drive. Jurors are deliberating in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position as city manager to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit co-founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. The defense denied Mimms did anything wrong, arguing that he and his niece, Caleta Scott, have a distant relationship. The prosecution argued there was a conflict of interest, saying Scott was granted special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms. Deliberations began late yesterday after closing arguments from both sides and resumed at 9 a.m. Jurors have broken for lunch but have not yet reached a verdict. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A West Palm Beach woman is turning her husband’s Huntington’s disease diagnosis into a mission to raise awareness and support families affected by the progressive neurological disease.Madison Donovan says her husband, Brian, was diagnosed with Huntington's disease at age 21, just four years ago. Now, she is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk this weekend outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.The walk is scheduled for Saturday at 9 a.m. and aims to raise both awareness and money for people and families affected by Huntington’s disease.According to Donovan, Huntington’s disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior.For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families."I want to spread awareness. It’s not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. It's something that is affecting everyday people," Donovan said.Donovan is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk as part of an effort to bring more attention to Huntington’s disease and raise funds for those affected by it.Proceeds from the event will benefit the Huntington’s Disease Society of America, Donovan said.The fundraising goal is $10,000. Donovan says organizers are already halfway to that goal.The event will take place Saturday at 9 a.m. outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student is in critical condition after being struck by an SUV while walking to school Wednesday morning in Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say the crash happened around 6 a.m. near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue. PSLPD says the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway, alongside construction barrels in the area. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. Police said the driver made a U-turn at the next available location where he could safely turn around. He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. Investigators have not observed any apparent signs of impairment involving the driver. Police emphasized that assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. The teen suffered life-threatening injuries and remains in critical condition. The investigation remains active. Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has dashcam, surveillance, or other video from the area around the time of the crash to contact PSLPD at 772-871-5000 .

Senate candidate Angie Nixon visited Fort Pierce on Tuesday to speak with voters about reproductive health care, the economy, and other issues as part of her campaign across Florida ahead of the general election. Nixon, who represents a Jacksonville-area district in the Florida House of Representatives and describes herself as a Democratic Socialist, is holding town hall meetings across the state to connect with voters. Planned Parenthood President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson hosted the Fort Pierce town hall, focusing on reproductive freedom and Florida's maternal mortality crisis. McGill Johnson and Nixon outlined the leadership they believe Florida families need, including protecting abortion access and expanding comprehensive health care services statewide. "Representative Nixon is a true champion for reproductive freedom," McGill Johnson said. "In the Senate, she is going to stand up for affordable health care and our right to make our own decisions about our own bodies." During the event, Nixon addressed a question about a proposed Islamic center approved for construction in Palm Beach County. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "This is a country where folks should have freedom of religion," Nixon said. "I would speak out against that type of opposition and hate if it was directed at a synagogue being built, if it was directed at a church being built, if it was directed at any other spiritual facility." Nixon also discussed the state of reproductive health care in Florida and other issues raised by voters. "Gas is high, people are struggling to get to and from work, and then they can't even afford the food anymore, let alone taking their children to the movies or out to eat, that's null and void now," one voter said. Nixon won the Democratic primary in St. Lucie County with about 54% of the vote. When asked how she plans to close the gap between herself and Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Nixon said she intends to continue engaging with voters, including those who may disagree with her. "They have someone who is going to put them first," Nixon said when asked about the message she hopes attendees took away from Tuesday's event. She added that her campaign for U.S. Senate is focused on putting money back in people's pockets. Nixon spoke with voters for about an hour. Her next stop is in the Orlando area. Matt Elliott wants to know whether his brain cancer could be connected to other diagnoses on the Treasure Coast. He also knows he may not live long enough to get an answer. It might take them years to even figure out what the hell’s going on around here, Elliott said. I can’t expect myself to be around at the end of it. Lucie County have raised similar questions for years, pointing to diagnoses just houses apart and, in some cases, among unrelated residents of the same home decades apart. In June, I-Team reporter Katie Bente revisited families’ search for answers. In this second part of her investigation, Bente went street by street with a widow tracking the diagnoses and pressing health officials for updated findings. A few houses apart For Stephanie Ankiel , one stop on the drive through Fort Pierce brings the questions back to her own family. She pointed to her late husband’s childhood home, then another home a few houses away where she said a resident was diagnosed in 2025 with the same type of brain tumor. This is the house my late husband grew up in, Ankiel said. He was diagnosed with the same exact thing as that gentleman in 2025. Both men were initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma, a different type of brain tumor from glioblastoma . Ankiel said her husband Mark Cunningham’s cancer later progressed to glioblastoma. A few streets away, she identified another home where she said two unrelated residents developed glioblastoma decades apart. This is the house where we’ve had two glioblastoma cases, 20 years apart, no family relation, she said. Elsewhere along the route, Ankiel pointed to neighboring homes where she said a woman and an 18-year-old had been diagnosed with brain cancer. The I-Team is withholding exact addresses to protect families’ privacy. PART 1: Brain cancer diagnoses leave St. Lucie County families searching for answers, again Ankiel helps patients through the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast , including a child who is just 3. She has spent years mapping where patients lived and looking for possible connections. Three additional brain cancer cases were confirmed in August alone in the areas families are tracking. Those diagnoses and the proximity of patients’ homes do not establish a cancer cluster or a common cause. But Ankiel wants officials to examine the range of brain cancers represented on her map, beyond glioblastoma alone. Regardless if it’s Glio at this point, we have too much brain cancer in this area. CDC guidance allows consideration of different cancer types when evidence suggests shared causes or exposures. No such connection has been established among the cases families are tracking. What the state studied and what is new The Florida Department of Health’s 2019 review examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 1998 through 2017 in ZIP codes 34952, 34982 and 34983. It found no statistically significant increase and did not designate a cancer cluster. That review did not include later diagnoses and focused on glioblastoma rather than the range of brain tumors represented on Ankiel’s map. Her husband’s initial diagnosis is one reason she wants officials to examine that broader picture. The I-Team asked whether the department had analyzed cases diagnosed since 2017 and what would trigger new environmental testing. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber said officials have been reviewing cancer registry data and environmental influences. Our latest analysis, which includes data through 2023, shows no indication of higher rates in St. Lucie County or in the specific zip codes people have asked about, Sperber wrote. Lucie’s rates are in line with nearby counties and with the state as a whole. The updated report was not available when he responded. Sperber said officials were finishing a summary to release online. His response did not explain how the analysis handled tumors initially classified as another type and later diagnosed as glioblastoma, or whether other brain cancers were examined separately. It also did not specify what would trigger additional environmental testing. No environmental factor questioned by families has been established as a cause of these cancers. A call for another look Rep. Brian Mast said he has again asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to examine the concerns and provide the data behind its conclusions. You need to give us the receipts, Mast said. Give us the data of where these took place, how many of them took place. The CDC said state and local health departments lead examinations of unusual cancer patterns. It confirmed that it assisted Florida’s investigation in 2018, but did not specifically address whether it had received Mast’s latest request or would open a new review. In a statement to the I-Team, a CDC spokesperson said: CDC is prepared to provide additional assistance upon the Florida Department of Health’s request. Making the most of the time left Elliott was diagnosed this year with glioblastoma, an aggressive, fast-growing grade 4 brain cancer. The former bar manager described struggling to speak after surgery and initially believing his diagnosis was an isolated case. Meeting other local patients changed that. I thought I was the only one, he said. He has decided not to continue treatment, choosing to spend his remaining time with friends and family, going to the beach and swimming. While he wants investigators to find answers, he is focused on the life he still has. I’m not going to be that person that lives to be 65, 70, 80 years old, Elliott said. But I get to hang out with my friends. I get to go take a swim, have some fun.

For nearly 40 years, The Golden Girls have entertained audiences with humor, friendship and unforgettable characters. Now, those beloved ladies are coming to South Florida through the touring stage production "Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue."The show arrives at the Raymond F. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach on Oct. 25, bringing Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia back together in a new story that imagines the iconic friends still living under one roof decades after the original sitcom ended.Actor Vince Kelley, who portrays Blanche Devereaux, and Adam Graber, who plays Rose Nylund, say the comedy's enduring popularity comes from its ability to connect with people from all walks of life."It's a very multifaceted answer," Kelley said. "The generational appeal, the nostalgia and stuff like that."He said the sitcom remains a source of comfort for viewers who return to the familiar characters again and again."Women of a certain age who sometimes can feel forgotten or cast aside, this gives them a voice," Kelley said. "The LGBT community obviously has very strong ties. Everybody can kind of identify with one of the girls, so it's easy to see yourself in the show."Full Interview with CastAlthough the original sitcom was set in Miami, the cast believes its themes resonate throughout South Florida."The lifestyle is born from this area," Kelley said. "We're going to be in West Palm Beach. How many people in West Palm Beach are retirees of a certain age who are maybe living this life, living with friends? They have a timeshare; they're doing this."The actors said audiences across Florida often recognize elements of their own communities in the world created by the television series."It's all South Florida," Kelley said. "The alligators, the humidity, banana leaves."The performers also said Florida audiences have embraced the production since it first began touring in the state."We always look forward to coming to Florida because of how solid the fan base is," Kelley said.The production imagines a continuation of the television series rather than a simple tribute show.According to the cast, Sophia has been arrested for operating a drug ring at Shady Pines, while Blanche and Rose launch a dating app for seniors. Meanwhile, Dorothy is forced into the world of online dating and begins a relationship with the very attorney prosecuting Sophia.The result is a fast-paced comedy that blends modern humor with the personalities fans have loved for decades.The show also embraces some of the continuity quirks that longtime viewers know well.During the interview, the actors laughed about references in the original sitcom that seemingly placed Jupiter's Burt Reynolds Dinner Theatre just a short drive from Miami."None of it makes sense," Graber joked. "You just let it happen."For many fans, The Golden Girls represents more than comedy.The cast said audience members frequently share personal stories during meet-and-greet events, telling them how the show connected them with parents, grandparents and close friends.Others describe finding comfort in the sitcom during difficult periods of their lives.That emotional connection continues to help new generations discover Dorothy, Blanche, Rose and Sophia long after the series left the air.Whether viewers tune in for the one-liners, the friendships, or the nostalgia, the cast believes the secret is simple: everyone can find a little of themselves in one of the four friends.Golden Girls: The Laughs Continue comes to the Kravis Center on Sunday, Oct. 25, with performances at 2 p.m. and 7:30 p.m.Organizers recommend buying tickets directly through Kravis.org to avoid scams and third-party resellers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia’s Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. “We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media,” Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia’s Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. “The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch,” Flowers said. “He’s going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case.” The teen’s friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff’s office’s Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. “There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting,” Flowers said. “Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there’s going to be more of this.” Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday’s news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim’s mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia’s Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. “When it’s Snapchat, it’s basically a private conversation,” Flowers said. “But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there.” Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. “Now we’re adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we’re adding social media into the mix, and so what we’re seeing is an escalation of each one of these,” Flowers said. There’s guns, and those two just don’t mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead.” The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. “The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that,” Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School’s homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children’s whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff’s office. “Parents, if your kids are telling you that they’re headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they’re going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us,” Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place. The investigation remains active. Flowers said anyone who witnessed any of the events that night, including the shooting itself, and has not yet spoken to investigators is urged to come forward. “I can tell you, our investigation is not even remotely over, and if we are able to identify people that were involved in this, from underage drinking to fighting, hurting other people,” Flowers said. " If they did something wrong, they’re going to have to be accountable for that." Anyone with information is asked to call the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office at 772-569-6700 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-TIPS.

A heated debate over Palm Beach County's investment in Israeli bonds unfolded Tuesday as residents packed commission chambers to voice support and opposition to the county's continued participation in the investment program. WATCH BELOW: Debate heats up over Israeli bond investmentThe county currently holds approximately $1 billion in Israeli bonds, making it the world's largest investor in the securities, according to county officials and speakers at the meeting.Supporters argued the investment provides strong financial returns for taxpayers while strengthening ties with a longtime U.S. Opponents said the county should reconsider the investments because of concerns related to Israel's military actions in the Middle East.The discussion comes as Palm Beach County is preparing for an additional $67 million investment in Israeli bonds scheduled to take effect Nov. 1.The debate drew passionate testimony from residents on both sides of the issue.At times, tensions escalated inside commission chambers, with law enforcement removing some attendees from the meeting.Opponents of the investment argued taxpayer funds should not be connected to actions they oppose overseas and called on county leaders to reconsider the county's involvement with Israeli bonds.Supporters countered that the bonds represent a sound financial investment that benefits Palm Beach County residents."This is not about political agenda. It's about investment that benefit all Palm Beach County citizens," said supporter Ifataloni. "We don't want to pay more taxes in here."Among those speaking against the investment was Lydia Singh."What it's about is making sure that no government gets special treatment," Singh said.She also argued county investments should be based on financial performance and fiduciary responsibility."Investments cannot be made for social or political reasons, and they must be made where it's the most prudent investment and most financially profitable investment possible," Singh said.While much of the discussion centered on county government, Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter said the county commission does not directly decide where investment funds are placed."We, the commission, do not decide where those investments get spent. The clerk of courts does," Baxter said.Baxter said she nevertheless chose to allow public comment on the issue because of the strong community interest surrounding the investments."Even though we don't decide, I still chose to let them speak," she said.One of the key arguments from supporters centered on the financial return generated by the investment.Baxter said she has been told the county's investment has produced a return of at least 5.7%."The numbers that I've heard are it's at least a 5.7% return on investment," Baxter said. "That's huge, and the amount of money that it brings into this county is amazing."She said the returns help generate revenue beyond property tax collections and can benefit county residents.The county's planned $67 million investment remains scheduled to take effect Nov. 1 as debate over the issue continues.WPTV will continue following developments and reactions from county leaders and residents.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense.The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A West Palm Beach woman is turning her husband’s Huntington’s disease diagnosis into a mission to raise awareness and support families affected by the progressive neurological disease.Madison Donovan says her husband, Brian, was diagnosed with Huntington’s disease at age 21, just four years ago. Now, she is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk this weekend outside the Spanish River Library in Boca Raton.The walk is scheduled for Saturday at 9 a.m. and aims to raise both awareness and money for people and families affected by Huntington’s disease.According to Donovan, Huntington’s disease is a hereditary and progressive neurological disease that can affect movement and behavior.For Donovan, the diagnosis has become a reason to help others better understand a disease she says affects everyday families.“I want to spread awareness. It’s not just a disease that goes into the rare disease book. It’s something that is affecting everyday people,” Donovan said.Donovan is helping organize the Hope for HD Walk as part of an effort to bring more attention to Huntington’s disease and raise funds for those affected by it.Proceeds from the event will benefit the Huntington’s Disease Society of America, Donovan said.The fundraising goal is $10,000.
