Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

President Donald Trump wants to transform Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach County into a permanent presidential retreat for U.S. presidents and visiting foreign leaders, a proposal that would involve county-owned land and a new lodging facility paid for by the golf club.The proposal, outlined in a Sept. 3 letter from Trump International Golf Club attorney Harvey E. Oyer to Palm Beach County commissioners, calls for the golf club to partner with the county and the federal government to create what Trump has described as a Camp David-style retreat.Trump announced the idea Wednesday, saying the concept was suggested by the military and U.S. Secret Service.“They could spend the weekend there like a retreat, like sort of a Camp David retreat,” Trump said. But the location presents a significant security question. Trump International Golf Club was the site of an attempted assassination of Trump in September 2024, when he was a presidential candidate. A former FBI agent who spoke with WPTV's Michael Hoffman says the property's location and surrounding roads could make it difficult to secure as a permanent presidential retreat.The golf club's letter asks Palm Beach County to designate Trump International Golf Club as the “permanent United States Presidential Golf Course.”Under the proposal, the club would make its golf courses and amenities available to past, current and future U.S. presidents, regardless of political party, as well as visiting foreign heads of state, at the discretion of the White House.The letter says Trump International Golf Club would work with the U.S. General Services Administration and U.S. Secret Service to design an appropriate presidential lodging facility.The club says it would pay the cost of constructing the lodging facility and provide access to the facilities at no cost to the federal government.Oyer described the proposal as a gift to future presidents and the American people, noting in the letter that Trump would be out of office before the project could be completed.The letter also points to the golf club's proximity to Palm Beach International Airport, South Florida's weather and existing security measures as reasons the property would be well suited for the proposal.The club called Trump International Golf Club “one of the most secure golf courses in the world” and described it as an ideal site for a presidential retreat.The golf course sits on county-owned land that is leased long term to Trump International Golf Club, according to the club's letter.Under the proposed arrangement, Trump International Golf Club would grant the county a legal right to the land needed for the lodging facility and other structures. The county would then lease that property to the federal government, allowing the county to remain the landlord.The proposal says Palm Beach County would retain control of the property if the federal government no longer wanted to use the facility or defaulted on its lease.That means the proposal would require more than simply building a new facility at the golf course. It would create a new arrangement among the golf club, Palm Beach County and the federal government.The proposal remains in its early stages. WPTV is reaching out to Palm Beach County commissioners about whether they support providing county land for the project.The proposal's security claims come with a notable complication: Trump International Golf Club was the scene of an attempted assassination of Trump on Sept. 15, 2024.Federal prosecutors said Ryan Wesley Routh was convicted in 2025 of attempting to assassinate Trump at the golf course. He was sentenced in February 2026 to life in federal prison plus seven years.According to the Justice Department, a Secret Service agent conducting a security sweep at the golf course spotted Routh along the fence line near the sixth hole with a rifle. The agent fired at Routh, who fled before being arrested in Martin County.The incident demonstrated the security challenges posed by the golf course's perimeter, including areas adjacent to public roads.Former FBI agent Stuart Kaplan told WPTV he believes securing the property as a permanent presidential retreat would be extremely difficult.“I think it would be absolutely impossible to secure the Trump International Golf Course,” Kaplan said.Kaplan pointed to the property's location near major thoroughfares and the need to secure both the perimeter and surrounding airspace.“If you're going to secure this type of retreat, it has to be 24 hours a day, seven days a week, all day long, every single day,” Kaplan said.Kaplan also questioned the need for a permanent presidential retreat in South Florida.Trump's proposal would ultimately require coordination between Palm Beach County, Trump International Golf Club and the federal government.The club has proposed paying for the lodging facility and says the arrangement would come at no cost to the federal government. Palm Beach County, however, would play a central role because the golf course sits on county-owned land.For now, the proposal is only that — a proposal. County commissioners have yet to determine whether they support the arrangement, and additional questions remain about the project's design, land agreement and security requirements.WPTV is seeking reaction from Palm Beach County commissioners as the proposal moves forward.Read the full letter here:

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

South Florida commuters are paying more to ride Tri-Rail after the regional rail service implemented a 10% fare increase, a move officials say is necessary as the agency works to address ongoing funding challenges.The fare hike, which took effect Oct. 1, increases one-way fares by roughly 30 cents to $1, depending on the route. Round-trip costs have increased by about $1 to $2, according to Tri-Rail.WATCH: Tri-Rail riders are paying more after a 10% fare increase.For many riders who rely on public transportation every day, the higher cost is already noticeable.The increase comes as transportation costs continue to rise for South Florida residents, with higher gasoline prices and other commuting expenses putting additional pressure on household budgets. For riders who depend on Tri-Rail to get to work, school and appointments, even modest fare increases can have a significant impact.Jordan Bruce, a regular Tri-Rail passenger, said he depends on the train to travel between West Palm Beach and Deerfield Beach."Some people don't have a choice, kind of like me right now," Bruce told WPTV.Bruce said the fare increase has been noticeable."I've definitely seen the price go up. It's very noticeable from before," he said.Without access to a car, Bruce said Tri-Rail remains a necessity."I really depend on the train. So let's say one day I don't have enough, I'm pretty much screwed that day," he said.Another rider, Daniel Presmr, said the need for reliable transportation outweighs the higher costs."At the end of the day, I gotta get home," Presmr said.Victor Garcia, director of public affairs for Tri-Rail, said the fare increase is intended to generate additional revenue, though it represents only a small portion of the agency's overall financial needs."That's one of the things that the board decided we had to do because, right, we got to look for all the means that we can to try to get more money," Garcia said.According to Garcia, the agency is still waiting for $45 million to $60 million in state funding. "That funding is essential for Tri-Rail services. It actually helps operate our train service," Garcia said.Tri-Rail officials say they continue to search for long-term funding solutions while monitoring future financial needs.Garcia said potential service reductions have been discussed if funding challenges persist."Some of the things that we had we've been considering is potentially like weekend service having to cut off," Garcia said.Despite the current fare increase, Tri-Rail officials said they do not anticipate another rate hike as they continue working to close the funding gap.Tri-Rail operates commuter rail service across Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties, providing a transportation alternative for thousands of South Florida riders each day.Garcia said keeping those riders on Tri-Rail also helps reduce congestion on South Florida roads."This is 15,000 people a day — the equivalent of about one lane of traffic on I-95. You throw them on the roads, now you’re dealing with that much more traffic," Garcia said.As Tri-Rail works to determine how to address its funding needs, Garcia said the larger question is how much the region is willing to invest in the service."Is Tri-Rail important to the region? And if it is, at what cost? If we know it’s a valuable service, then we need to support it to keep it going," he said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. WPTV is taking a closer look at the military operation protecting the skies above Palm Beach County and the number of aircraft that have crossed into restricted airspace around Mar-a-Lago since President Donald Trump returned to office.According to the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, fighter pilots have intercepted more than 60 aircraft violating Temporary Flight Restrictions around Palm Beach since January 2025.WATCH BELOW: NORAD intercepted 60+ aircraft near Mar-a-Lago since 2025"Since January of 2025, there have been over 60 intercepts that we've had to accomplish," said Major Anthony Olive, an F-15 pilot and senior operations duty officer with NORAD.When announcing the number during a media briefing held Tuesday at President Donald J. Trump International Airport, Olive's reaction was immediate."I would say so. I would say that's a lot," said Olive.The briefing comes as WPTV continues reporting on the impact the restrictions have had on communities below, including concerns about increased aircraft noise in parts of West Palm Beach and Palm Beach.In May, Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss told WPTV the rerouted flight paths have impacted approximately 20,000 residents.The restrictions, known as TFRs, are routinely put in place when Trump is staying at Mar-a-Lago. NORAD officials told WPTV they do not create the restrictions. Instead, the restrictions are established by the Federal Aviation Administration and U.S. Secret Service, while NORAD is responsible for enforcing them."We're here to enforce the TFR and to ensure the safety of everyone, to include the individuals on the ground, the airplanes that are flying in the air as well, to make sure nobody violates the TFR, and if they do, to make sure that they're escorted safely out of the TFR as well, basically to keep the airspace clean," Olive said.NORAD officials shared a demonstration video where WPTV was given a close look at the fighter aircraft and personnel responsible for protecting the restricted airspace.Pilots assigned to the mission are not waiting on the ground for a violation to occur.When asked whether they launch after a violation or patrol routinely, one pilot's answer was simple:"Regularly patrol," the pilot replied.Officials said fighter jets are already in position before the restrictions take effect."When the TFR goes active, we're already airborne, and we're there," Olive said.If a pilot enters restricted airspace without authorization, NORAD receives notification through air traffic control."We're already airborne. They'll give us a point out; we'll find it with our radar, we'll go check it out, and basically get their intention, what they're looking to do," Olive said. "If they're just a person who doesn't know they're not supposed to be there, then we'll help escort them out of the TFR safely."Despite the number of interceptions, officials said the overwhelming majority involve pilots making mistakes, not people attempting to threaten the restricted airspace."I would say the majority, that is correct," Olive said. "There's also a majority of it where they have the proper code, they have the proper clearance, they just forget to squawk the right code, so they take off, they have a clearance, they're good to go, but they haven't punched in that clearance in their airplane, and then they do so on departure, but we still have to scramble on them because we don't know their intention because they're not squawking the right code."Asked whether any of the interceptions he has handled involved bad intentions, Olive said: "Not, I don't, no, not from my experience, no, they're just people who forget or who have not done the proper flight planning."Officials say most of the aircraft involved are not large commercial jets."The majority would be smaller Cessnas, single-engine planes for sure," said Olive.Palm Beach presents unique challenges, according to NORAD, because of the large amount of general aviation traffic in the area."I'd say Mar-a-Lago is interesting. It's different from up north," one pilot said. "There's more general aviation down here due to the nice weather, the amount of flight schools that are around here, people want to fly up and down the coast, the banner towers, so we get more general aviation traffic down here for sure."The restricted airspace itself consists of two zones."It's a temporary flight restriction," a pilot explained. "It encompasses a 10-mile ring centered at the airfield here, and then there's a 30-mile ring as well that extends beyond that. The 10-mile ring is essentially a no-fly zone."Pilots operating inside the larger ring must follow special FAA procedures."You have to be on a flight plan. You have to be squawking a discrete code, and in comms with ATC."Officials emphasized that while most violations are innocent mistakes, every response is treated seriously."We're always training to take it all the way to the conclusion that, hey, this is a person with bad intentions," Olive said. "Obviously that is a last, last resort. We're not there to hand down the judgment or the punishment; we're just there to enforce the TFR and escort them safely either to land or outside of the TFR."Any penalties are handled by the FAA once the aircraft lands."We'll safely escort them out. We'll make sure that they land. We'll monitor them until they land at their destination," Olive said. "Upon landing, they'll be notified that they have a phone number to call that'll be a phone number that leads them to the FAA and then the FAA will deal with that."Officials also stressed how closely NORAD and the FAA work together."It's imperative. We're completely intertwined," Olive said. "The FAA, they can't do their job without us. We can't do our job without them."For residents wondering why military aircraft may be overhead during presidential visits, officials say the mission comes down to safety."Any time you have the president of the United States travel anywhere, that's a very high visibility movement, and it attracts a lot of attention not only within the United States but nationally as well," one pilot said.And for pilots flying near Palm Beach, NORAD had a straightforward message:"If you're going to fly, if you're an avid flyer, check your NOTAMs before you fly, just so everybody's safe, and you're not where you're not supposed to be."When asked whether he had a message for Trump himself, the pilot smiled."Yeah, sir, we'll be above you, keeping you safe in the sky."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. WPTV is listening to concerns about what could come next following a lot of controversy surrounding a proposed Islamic center, school and daycare in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve near Delray Beach.Now, WPTV's Joel Lopez is getting answers from Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs, who is asking county staff to review how some projects, including places of worship, receive approval, a move that could affect how similar projects are handled in the future.WATCH BELOW: Islamic Center controversy prompts county review of approval processThe proposed development near Lyons Road in Delray Beach has sparked public debate for months, with residents raising concerns about the project and whether projects of that nature should receive additional public scrutiny.During a recent county commission meeting, Sachs asked county staff to review portions of the county's land development code involving government facilities and places of worship."I would like board direction to staff to research and prepare a presentation on government services and places of worship uses with draft revisions to the ULDC to require their approval as a Class A conditional use approval before the BCC," Sachs said.Later in the discussion, Sachs explained why she wants staff to take another look at the current process."For many years, any government facilities or places of worship were able to get approval through DRO, which is an administrative approval through the zoning staff, and never came before the board for a hearing," Sachs said.Sachs stressed she is not proposing an immediate change to county rules, but to begin the first steps in the process."I'm asking the staff to review that and bring it back to us for a presentation and our consensus on it and what we think about it," Sachs said.The discussion comes as residents continue to question how the proposed Islamic center moved through the approval process."The issue is whether or not we are going to bring all classifications back to the board as opposed to singling out places of worship," said County attorney David Ottey.Lopez has been digging into this project and learned that the school and daycare portion of the project went before county commissioners in 2023. Sachs, then-Commissioner Sara Baxter and former Commissioner Michael Barnett voted against the proposal, but it was ultimately approved in a 4-3 vote.Commissioners Maria Marino, Marci Woodward, Gregg Weiss and then-Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor, allowing the project to move forward.The proposed mosque on an adjacent parcel, however, did not come before county commissioners because places of worship can currently be approved administratively by county staff.That process was the focus of several public comments during Tuesday's meeting.One resident urged county commissioners to revisit the issue."Please consider the vote that was made in 2023," said Pamela Higer-Polani, an attorney who lives in the Ag Reserve. "There is precedent that if this body, this esteemed body, reevaluates its decision, you have it within your power to open up the vote again. We are asking you to do so and reconsider."Another resident questioned whether the project has already obtained legal protections that could make changes difficult."My question is whether those approvals have become legally vested and immune from subsequent action from this commission," the resident said.The resident also asked county officials to answer several legal questions publicly, including if the projects will grandfather development rights, and if construction has not commenced and vested rights have not been established, could a moratorium or new Agricultural Reserve development restrictions adopted by the commission legally apply to this project.WPTV got answers from Sachs, who told WPTV that any changes to the approval process would not affect projects that have already received county approval."If we are able to get these amendments passed, do you think that's going to change the projects going forward?" asked Lopez."It won't change any project that's already been approved," answered Sachs.Sachs said changing the status of previously approved projects would likely require legal action. She also said she is considering a moratorium on new applications, and those in the works while county staff reviews the current process and prepares recommendations for commissioners."My message is very clear: I hear your voices, I know that you're upset, and I understand that, and actually I agree," Sachs said. "This has been an issue, and this is something we need to clear up."Not everyone speaking during public comment opposed the project.Rabbi Steve Moss urged county leaders and residents to support religious freedom regardless of faith."As faith leaders and citizens of Delray Beach, we value living in a pluralistic, respectful democracy where faith communities can live side-by-side in peace," Moss said.Moss also defended the ability of religious groups to build facilities in the community."We join communities throughout our country in standing together and defending every faith community's right to build houses of worship and community centers," Moss said.Questions were also raised by commissioners about the legal implications of changing approval standards for houses of worship.Commissioner Maria Marino asked county attorneys whether federal protections could limit what the county can do."Before we go this route, I would like clarification on what we can and can't do when it comes to a religious use or a place of worship," Marino said.County attorneys told commissioners they would return with research and legal analysis, including any federal and state legal considerations.For now, no code changes have been approved, and no action has been taken against previously approved projects. County staff is expected to review the issue and bring findings and recommendations back to commissioners for future discussion.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The incident occurred on National Walk, Bike, & Roll to School Day . Lucie flooding problem renews focus on city's stormwater spending Officers said the teen was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. The driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person, according to investigators. Police said the driver made a U-turn at the next available location where he could safely turn around. He returned to the area, activated his hazard lights, and found the teen unconscious on the side of the road. The driver called 911 and has remained cooperative with investigators, police said. A former CIA agent convicted Tuesday of defrauding the government of $194 million reportedly used the majority of the money to acquire properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound. According to CBS Miami , court filings say 49-year-old David J. Rush of Virginia, a former high-ranking federal employee, directed $145 million to a holding company he controlled, and that $102 million was used to purchase four Florida properties: Two Palm Beach homes: $21.9 million and $27 million One Palm Beach parcel: $13.65 million One Hobe Sound parcel: $40 million Prosecutors allege Rush intended to eventually resell the properties for a profit. How the scheme unfolded According to the Department of Justice , Rush, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty Tuesday, Oct. 6, to wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia. According to prosecutors, Rush used his senior-level government position and "Top Secret" clearance to create fictitious government authorities and obtain federal money for his own benefit. Between November 2025 and March 2026, he directed approximately $145 million to a holding company established at his direction, according to court documents. The money was then used to purchase the properties. The Justice Department says Rush fraudulently obtained approximately $193.6 million in government funds. The South Florida real estate was only part of the alleged scheme. Gold bars Prosecutors say Rush separately created a fake "sensitive government activity" to justify acquiring hundreds of gold bars. On May 19, 2026, FBI agents searched Rush's Virginia home and recovered 298 gold bars, approximately $2.1 million in cash, €104,795, and numerous luxury watches. The gold had cost the government approximately $46 million, according to the Justice Department. Rush has agreed to forfeit the gold bars and cash, the Florida properties, luxury watches, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles as part of his plea agreement. What's next Rush is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. He faces a maximum of 20 years in federal prison, along with possible restitution, forfeiture and a fine. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing. The Director of National Intelligence has also requested an investigation by the Intelligence Community's inspector general. The allegations and admissions are detailed in federal court documents filed as part of Rush's guilty plea.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.Instead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find another place to stay if they can, and that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said that work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, pumps for canals, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from a $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment, which the city's website lists as proposed. That would raise the assessment from $183 to $189. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

The city of Westlake is considering installing speed enforcement cameras in a school zone near Seminole Ridge High School, a proposal that city leaders say would improve student safety.The topic is expected to come before the Westlake City Council during its meeting Tuesday at 6 p.m., as officials discuss a potential agreement with RedSpeed, the company that would provide the camera technology.WATCH BELOW: Westlake considers speed cameras near Seminole Ridge HighAccording to Westlake City Manager Howard Brown Jr., the city has been discussing school zone speed cameras for about a year. A speed zone study conducted by the city found a need for additional enforcement in the area surrounding Seminole Ridge High School."Seminole Ridge High School will be the target area," Brown said.City officials say the cameras would serve as an additional tool to address speeding drivers in the school zone."Some people are busy, and they are not paying attention that they are going through a school zone," Brown said.Brown, who has a young child at home, said protecting children is a top priority."I have a little one at home. That's an area where we really want to protect our children and provide law enforcement with additional tools," he said.Under the proposal, drivers caught traveling more than 10 mph over the posted speed limit on Seminole Pratt Whitney Road within the school zone would face a $100 citation."We are trying to break some of those bad driving habits," Brown said.Not everyone is convinced the cameras are necessary.Westlake resident Nicole Haley said she worries speed cameras could worsen existing traffic congestion."I think it would back up traffic even more than it already is," Haley said.Instead of adding cameras, Haley believes roadway improvements may be a better solution."I think integrating a roundabout like the one they have on Stribling would be better," she said.If approved, the cameras could be operational before the end of the year. The city says there would also be a 30-day warning period before citations are issued.At this time, Seminole Ridge High School is the only school in the city being considered for speed camera enforcement.The speed camera discussion is one of several items on Tuesday night's council agenda. City officials have also indicated they will not move forward with license plate reader technology at this time. The meeting will be held at the Lodge at 6 p.m.

Florida has reported nearly 500 dengue cases this year, including more than 250 infections acquired within the state, as new University of Florida research points to residential yards in Indian River County as a key place to understand mosquito-bite exposure. The Florida Department of Health’s latest weekly surveillance report , covering Sept. 20-26, lists 252 locally acquired dengue cases and 245 travel-associated cases statewide 497 total. The locally acquired cases were reported in Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas and Polk counties. Palm Beach County had one locally acquired case and 12 travel-associated cases; St. Lucie County had six travel-associated cases. No locally acquired dengue cases were listed for Indian River County in the report. The state’s locally acquired total includes 223 cases in Hillsborough County, the center of Florida’s outbreak. Health officials also reported 20 mosquito pools testing positive for dengue statewide. Nationally, the CDC’s most recent weekly provisional report counted 690 dengue cases among U.S. Florida accounted for 403 of those cases in the CDC reporting system, though the state’s more current surveillance report lists a higher total because reporting systems update on different schedules. Against that backdrop, researchers at UF/IFAS’ Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory in Vero Beach found a surprising mosquito pattern in suburban Indian River County. The team expected residential yards to be dominated by Aedes albopictus , also known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Instead, researchers found relatively high numbers of Aedes aegypti the yellow fever mosquito and one of the two species most closely associated with dengue transmission worldwide. The finding does not mean dengue is circulating in Indian River County . But it underscores why backyard mosquito control and personal bite prevention matter, researchers said. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf The first-of-its-kind study paired mosquito trapping at homes with a smartphone-based Bite Diary that let residents document when and where they were bitten. Researchers collected 3,788 female mosquitoes from 78 yards. Of 70 reported bites, nearly 93% happened outdoors and nearly 74% happened at home, according to the peer-reviewed study . The number of mosquitoes trapped in a yard was not associated with the number of bites residents reported. Instead, people who spent more time outside during the evening, from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m., reported more bites. Gardening and walking dogs were among activities commonly reported when bites occurred. Dengue is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person; it does not spread directly from person to person. Symptoms can include fever, severe muscle and joint pain, rash, nausea and pain behind the eyes. People with symptoms should contact a health care provider, especially after travel to an area where dengue is common. Health officials urge residents to use EPA-registered insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants when practical, repair window and door screens, and dump standing water from containers such as buckets, flowerpots, toys, tires and pool covers.

Governor Ron DeSantis was in Indian River County on Monday to celebrate the completion of a new I-95 interchange at Oslo Road, a $100 million project state officials say will improve traffic flow, emergency response times and freight movement. The interchange, which opened about a year ahead of schedule, marks the first new I-95 interchange built in Indian River County in nearly 50 years. DeSantis said the project will provide a new direct connection to I-95 while easing congestion at nearby interchanges at Indrio Road and State Road 60. “This is going to bring a new critical connection to I-95 for a part of the state that has changed quite a bit,” DeSantis said. According to the governor, drivers using Oslo Road to access I-95 can expect travel times to be cut roughly in half. State transportation officials also project traffic along the corridor will continue growing through 2045. DeSantis said the project is expected to have significant public safety benefits as well. The state estimates emergency response times in the area could be reduced by as much as 56%, allowing first responders to reach crashes and other emergencies more quickly. “This will ultimately save some lives because time is of the essence in some of these situations,” DeSantis said. Florida Department of Transportation Secretary Jared Perdue said improved access to I-95 for first responders was one of the project’s most important features. “Every single second counts when it comes to saving lives, and this is going to reduce the time it takes for first responders to get to incidents substantially,” Perdue said. The new interchange is also expected to improve freight movement for businesses in southern Indian River County by providing a more direct route to the interstate for trucks and commercial traffic. State officials said the project was accelerated through Florida’s Moving Florida Forward initiative, a transportation funding program launched by the DeSantis administration to speed up major road projects across the state. Perdue said FDOT worked with contractors through a “voluntary acceleration” program that rewarded construction teams for finding ways to complete projects more quickly. As a result, the Oslo Road interchange was finished approximately 400 days ahead of schedule. In addition to transportation improvements, FDOT acquired land near the interchange to establish a dedicated gopher tortoise habitat. State officials said the site will serve as the only relocation area of its kind in Southeast Florida, allowing protected tortoises to be moved while infrastructure projects continue. The Oslo Road interchange is part of nearly $1 billion in planned transportation investments across Florida’s Treasure Coast region. “This interchange sets a clear example of how Florida delivers infrastructure that improves quality of life today while building more capacity for the future,” DeSantis said.

After viewer videos showed water covering roads and vehicles struggling through several Port St. Lucie neighborhoods, the city's own budget documents show where it plans to put money to reduce flooding. The city says that work is still in its early stages. Lucie has received about 4 inches of rain over the past 48 hours , and another 2 to 4 inches could fall by the end of the week. City crews are monitoring conditions as water recedes, and officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay out of flooded roads because it is hard to tell how deep the water is. Frank Camarda, who has lived in the area for more than 20 years near SW California Boulevard and SW Plantation Terrace, said Tuesday night's flooding turned his street into a detour. He said drivers piled in while trying to bypass flooded roads, and he believes Savona Boulevard was also underwater. Camarda said he has not seen flooding on his own street before, but he has watched water pool near Oak Hammock a couple of times. He also said city crews used to clean the swale in front of his home about once a month, and he believes that has stopped. "I've been waiting for these guys to clean up. I haven't seen them," Camarda said. City spokesperson Scott Samples said the rain came in too fast for the system to keep up. He said the canals, swales and retention ponds were already full, which makes it harder for water to move. At one location the city monitored, he said, about two feet of water arrived in roughly 30 minutes. Samples said the water had receded from most roadways by about 8:30 p.m. Tuesday, and he described that as the stormwater system doing what it is designed to do. He said Public Works checks drainage before heavy rain and is working to keep swales, drains and canals clear, but there is only so much crews can do when that much water arrives at once. See also: Florida stages emergency supplies as Tropical Storm Isaias strengthens in Gulf Samples said residents who cannot get home should find another place to stay if they can, and that the city is working closely with police on safety. The city's proposed capital plan for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, submitted to City Council on April 13, includes the Oak Hammock Watershed Improvement Project. It would add new retention ponds, pump systems and upgraded valves. The plan shows $8 million in each of the first two years and $7 million in each of the next two, for $30 million in all, paid for through stormwater bond financing. Samples said the city has just begun early data analysis for Oak Hammock, which he placed in the California Boulevard area. He said that work will guide the design of a multi-phase project that could include new retention ponds, pumps for canals, or even raising the roadway at California and Savona boulevards so water drains off. He said it is hard to predict when residents will see construction or a finished project, because the city must first gather data, settle on a design and line up funding. He called Oak Hammock a priority for the city. "It will move as fast as it possibly can," Samples said. According to the city, the project covers a large area east of Interstate 95, north of the C-23 Canal and Port St. Lucie Boulevard, and west of Florida's Turnpike. The money would come partly from a $6 increase in the annual stormwater assessment, which the city's website lists as proposed. That would raise the assessment from $183 to $189. The city says the assessment helps pay for five projects aimed at flooding and water flow: Oak Hammock, the Elkcam Basin, the E-8 Canal, Hogpen Slough, and faster replacement of swales and culverts. The city says its drainage system includes about 200 miles of canals, 1,200 miles of swales, and more than 6,000 culverts. It also notes that maintaining swales and driveway culverts, from the edge of the pavement to the property line, is the property owner's responsibility under city code.

It takes an army of 38 staff members to create all the video, replays and entertainment fans enjoy at Florida Panthers games at Amerant Bank Arena.WPTV Florida Panthers anchor and Panthers 360 Mike Trim went one-on-one with Mike Masino, vice president of entertainment and operations, who gave Trim a tour of the newly renovated control room and front-of-house operations. WATCH: Newly renovated control room at Amerant Bank Arena brings Panthers games to lifeThe front-of-house operations area serves as the hub of game-day activity. It houses the public address announcer, primary producer, music operations, a spotter, and a gold horn operator. Lighting operations and building lights are also managed from the same space, along with social media stations used for interactive fan games."Yeah, so this is our front-of-house operations area. This is where we have our public address announcer. We have our primary producer, music operations, our spotter, and our gold horn operator. We've got our lighting operations team as well as building lights. And then up here we have some of our fun stuff. We've got social media stations for some of our interactive games," Mike Masino said.What is now one open workspace was once 3 separate rooms."This was actually 3 rooms," Masino said."Flow communication becomes a lot easier. Direct line of sight is also helpful, and it actually created some more space for the operators," Masino said.The tour also included the broadcast control room — the engine room of the entire production."Now we've got the actual broadcast control room; this is where the real magic happens," Masino said.Inside, Mark serves as the technical director, and Scott is the director. Masino compared the director's role to one familiar to those in television news."Mark, who's TDing, and you've got Scott who is our director. Our director, just like in news, is actually calling the cameras, calling the angles. Queuing videos," Masino said.When Trim asked how the team handles milestone moments — whether anticipated or unexpected — Masino said the control room is always plugged in and prepared."We're directly plugged in with our public relations team and our communications team, who communicate that milestone to us. We're prepared ahead of time," Masino said.Masino noted that the 38-person team is a critical part of the operation, pointing to significant growth in both staff size and talent."We've doubled the staff. Talent level is continuing to increase every year, and it's really become a wonderful, wonderful team," Masino said."They're on it. They're locked in all game, but it's what they do, and it's what they love to do," Masino said.The first pre-season game for the Panthers also marked a significant technology upgrade for the arena."So tonight's actually a milestone for us, moving from a baseband video infrastructure where you're hard patching cables to a networked routable video infrastructure," Masino said."All of our cabling throughout the building was replaced to bring us to the highest quality broadcast infrastructure that sports are doing these days," Masino said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. WPTV is working to get answers to questions residents raised about a controversial Islamic center approved in Palm Beach County's Agricultural Reserve. After Friday's heated public meeting, many viewers reached out asking who is behind the project, how it was approved and what happens next.The proposed development would be located off Lyons Road and 152nd Place South in Delray Beach, on what is currently a dirt road and grassy field. The project includes a mosque, school and daycare.WATCH BELOW: Who's behind the Ag Reserve Islamic Center? Residents seek answersDuring Friday's meeting, several residents questioned who is involved with the project and where funding is coming from. One speaker told county leaders, "If credible documented evidence exists connecting specific individuals or organizations associated with this project to extremist organizations, residents deserve to know what authorities have investigated and determined. Who controls this organization? Who is financing this project? Where is the money coming from? And what security review has been conducted?"The project also drew protesters outside the meeting."Where are they from, who are they, were they vetted? Build it and they shall come," said a woman pushing back against the Islamic center, calling the developments part of a "Muslim takeover."Sachs pushed through the feedback from the crowd and said places of worship of all faiths go through a review process."Yes, an investigation was made into every house of worship, whether it is Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu and we do have Hindu temples if anybody here is interested," Sachs said. there's an investigation made as to who owns it, who's going to run it, and whether or not they're going to abide by the rules of the county and the United States Constitution."Inside the meeting, a woman who identified herself as a Latina Muslim convert questioned the nature of the concerns being raised. Her comments drew a strong reaction from the crowd as some wanted to focus on traffic impacts and nearly caused the meeting to be shut down."I want to be safer again; will this development help my community to be safe? My mosque welcomes people of other faith to ask questions," she said.Questions about who is behind the project have remained a focal point for residents.The project consists of a 15-acre Islamic center featuring 5 acres for the mosque and 10 for the school and daycare along Lyons Road.County documents reviewed by WPTV appear to identify the applicant as the Islamic Center School of west Delray Beach. The organization also appears to own an additional 5 acres on the north side of 152nd Place South. Plans for that portion are uncertain.Seeking more context on the concerns raised at the meeting, WPTV spoke with former Rabbi David Steinhardt, who retired about 16 months ago after serving for more than 30 years as senior rabbi at B'nai Torah Congregation in Boca Raton. He also served as co-president of the Boca Raton Interfaith Clergy Association.When asked what his message would be to residents expressing concern about a mosque coming into the area and the impacts on the Jewish community, Steinhardt said, "No one's trying to take their place. The issue is how do we live together."He said fear often grows when people lack familiarity with one another."I think that when you don't know people, then you suspect people, and when you're suspicious, you fear people. And so when you fear people, then you don't necessarily act rationally. This is not a new group of people. These are people that have been in town for decades. We have worked together at the hospitals, in the courts, in business, in all different arenas of public uh public uh society. And in our community, we have shared in various efforts to bring peace to the world. And so, I know that community. I have been in conversation with that community and its leadership for decades."Steinhardt said he knows the president of the mosque approved for the site and said they are members of the Islamic Center of Boca Raton seeking a second mosque to provide better access for members."I don't know if it's a need, if it's a desire; that should be enough. Is there a need for the number of synagogues we have in our Community? I'm not sure, but there's a desire for more, and we all have the right to do that."WPTV also learned the project is represented by Brian Seymour with the Gunster law firm. A request for additional details has been sent, and WPTV is working to hear back.Another issue repeatedly raised Friday involved notification requirements. Several residents questioned why people living more than 500 feet from the site were not notified.The county's Planning and Zoning Division told WPTV that only property owners within 500 feet were notified because the project is located within the U/S, AGR and Glades tiers. Had the project been located within the Exurban and Rural tiers, a 1,000-foot notification radius would have applied.To see which growth tier a property falls under, open the Palm Beach County GIS Map Viewer. Once you're in the map, click the menu icon (the "pancake" in the upper corner), then use the "Search Layers" tool and type in "Managed Growth Tier System." That layer will show all of the county's designated growth tiers and allow you to see exactly where a property is located within the system.Palm Beach County Commissioner Maria Sachs is planning a second public meeting focused on projects in the Agricultural Reserve following feedback from Friday's meeting. Her staff told WPTV details are still being worked out.Sachs also told WPTV she is working with county staff to find an appropriate date to propose changes to the Unified Land Development Code regarding the Development Review Officer process for places of worship and governmental entities.The issue has become a focal point because several projects residents protested were approved through an administrative review process that has existed for years and allows certain government entities and houses of worship to move forward without direct approval from county commissioners."I think for the most part people had their voices heard, but what they said is they want to have a voice in what comes to development in this county. I respect that I hear them," Sachs said Friday.While the mosque was approved through the administrative process, the proposal for an Islamic school and daycare next door did require a vote by county commissioners.WPTV reviewed records from a 2023 county meeting and learned the project was approved by a 4-3 vote.Sachs, former Commissioner Michael Barnett and then-Commissioner Sara Baxter voted against the proposal, citing concerns that not enough input from residents had been collected.Vice Mayor Marci Woodward, Commissioner Maria Marino, Commissioner Gregg Weiss and former Commissioner Mack Bernard voted in favor of the project.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

No arrests have been made in the shooting death of a 17-year-old at a teen meetup near Garcia’s Boat Ramp in Indian River County, with a self-defense claim expected in the case, Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Monday. “We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media,” Flowers said. The shooting occurred late Friday night when approximately 100 teens, ranging in age from 14 to 19, gathered at Garcia’s Boat Ramp in the 3700 block of County Road 512, the sheriff said. Deputies had broken up a similar group earlier that evening before the crowd moved to the boat ramp. “The 17-year-old, and a group of his friends, are approaching a truck, and there are two people, both 18 years old, inside of that truck. The 17-year-old opens the door, and he starts to punch,” Flowers said. “He’s going to punch on the people that are inside of that truck. That shot is the shot that ultimately killed 17-year-old in this case.” The teen’s friends drove him away from the scene, east on County Road 512, while calling 911 and a dispatcher told them to stop at Fellsmere City Hall, where emergency crews performed CPR, the sheriff said. He was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later flown to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he died from his injuries. The two individuals in the truck were identified using the sheriff’s office’s Flock technology, the sheriff said. Flowers said both have been cooperative with investigators, surrendering the weapon used in the shooting and the truck. Additional individuals involved in the incident have also been identified through Flock, though some remain unidentified. Investigators also recovered other weapons from the vehicle in which the 17-year-old was transported from the scene. Flowers said a warrant will be submitted in the case, but it will be up to the state to determine whether charges are filed. “There have been no arrests on this case at this time, because the preliminary investigation shows that the 17-year-old was opening the door to attempt to fight with the two that were inside of the vehicle. They had a history of fighting,” Flowers said. “Self defense plays a part in these, and when these kids go out and videotape these fights, and now guns are involved, there’s going to be more of this.” Names of those involved are not being released as the investigation continues, the sheriff said. Investigators believe at least four fights occurred at the boat ramp on the night of the shooting. Multiple shell casings and rounds were recovered from the scene. During Monday’s news conference, Flowers released video of the shooting, noting the footage had already circulated widely on social media and that the victim’s mother had seen it. One of the 18-year-olds involved in the shooting attends Vero Beach High School. The sheriff said teen meetups like the one at Garcia’s Boat Ramp are coordinated through Snapchat, making them difficult for law enforcement to track in advance. “When it’s Snapchat, it’s basically a private conversation,” Flowers said. “But it quickly can escalate to over 100, 150, 200 people there.” Flowers said the meetups, which have included alcohol, fighting, and firearms, have been taking place for years across Indian River County, Okeechobee, and surrounding areas, but that social media has intensified the danger. “Now we’re adding guns and alcohol into the mix, and we’re adding social media into the mix, and so what we’re seeing is an escalation of each one of these,” Flowers said. There’s guns, and those two just don’t mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead.” The sheriff said teens at these gatherings are motivated in part by a desire for online attention. “The kids like to fight, and they like to videotape it, and they like to get their likes and shares because of that,” Flowers said. Parents, you see these videos. You do not want your teens out at these meetups." With Vero Beach High School’s homecoming game scheduled for Friday and the dance on Saturday, Flowers said additional deputies will be on duty. Meanwhile, the sheriff urged parents to monitor their children’s whereabouts and report any information about planned meetups to the sheriff’s office. “Parents, if your kids are telling you that they’re headed out to one of these meetups, ask them where they’re going. Ask, find out the details. Share that with us,” Flowers said. He recommended parents use location-sharing apps such as Life360 to track their children and said a child appearing to be in a remote or unusual location can be an indicator that a meetup is taking place.
